lessons.title: Assessment authority, scope and decision criteria
lessons.body:
An OT assessment is a decision process supported by technical evidence. Begin with the decision the owner must make: accept a new remote-maintenance service, approve a plant expansion, prioritize replacement of unsupported controllers, or determine whether a recovery architecture is adequate. A list of vulnerabilities without this decision context gives little basis for allocating engineering effort. Write the decision, accountable owner, assessment date, system configuration baseline and required outputs before selecting tools.

Define three boundaries separately. The system boundary identifies the assets, functions and dependencies being evaluated. The assessment activity boundary identifies what assessors may inspect or test. The consequence boundary identifies who or what can be harmed if the system behaves incorrectly. These boundaries need not coincide. A corporate identity service outside the team's administrative control can authorize a command inside the assessed plant. A cooling controller in one hall can affect adjacent halls through a shared water loop. An assessment may need to model both dependencies while obtaining evidence through their respective owners rather than probing them directly.

The charter should name asset owners, process operators, safety personnel, IT identity/network teams, integrators and vendors where their evidence is necessary. Record who can authorize a collection activity, who can stop it, and who may accept residual risk. These are different authorities. An assessor may identify a risk and recommend treatment without possessing authority to accept business or process consequences. A commissioning engineer's ability to change a switch configuration is not authority to perform an unscheduled vulnerability scan.

Translate operational constraints into observable rules. 'Do not disrupt the plant' is too vague. A collection plan could require passive capture from an approved mirror port, no packets transmitted onto the control segment, collector CPU below its platform-specific limit, a bounded capture duration, and an operator present to watch specified health indicators. An authorized active test needs a source, destination list, protocol or plugin list, rate ceiling, time window, restoration plan, stop conditions and a communication path independent of the network under test. These values come from the owner and representative testing; a universal 'safe scan rate' does not exist.

Set assessment criteria before examining results. Specify consequence categories such as personnel injury, environmental release, cooling interruption, data loss and financial impact. Do not collapse a life-safety consequence into a financial equivalent merely to obtain one score. Define the likelihood scale and its time horizon, how existing safeguards will be credited, what evidence supports a judgment, and how uncertainty will be reported. Distinguish an initial screening decision from a detailed assessment; an initial qualitative rating may prioritize further work without pretending to be a measured incident probability.

A useful scope register has columns for function, asset or service, owner, physical location, trust relationships, inclusion status, evidence route and rationale. 'Excluded from active testing; included as a dependency' is a legitimate status. 'Out of scope' without a rationale hides attack paths. Freeze an initial baseline and record changes, because a risk conclusion about firmware A and remote-access configuration B may not apply after either changes.

Finally, define deliverables and review gates. The charter should require a current architecture, inventory with confidence labels, consequence model, vulnerability findings with applicability analysis, scenario-based risks, a treatment plan, residual-risk ownership, and traceable cybersecurity requirements where design follows. These are engineering artifacts that another reviewer can challenge and reproduce. The assessment itself does not certify a security level, prove safety, or award an ISA qualification.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. Directory administration is outside the OT team's control. The sponsor asks whether vendor remote maintenance may be enabled before summer. Approved collection: read-only configuration exports and a 20-minute passive mirror-port capture on OT switch S1. No active packets are authorized. Cooling alarms must remain visible; the duty operator may stop collection. The facility director owns acceptance of service interruption risk; the assessor reports findings. A draft scope excludes D1 because it is 'an IT asset'.
worked_examples.solution:
The decision is whether the proposed remote-maintenance arrangement can be accepted with defined controls before a seasonal operating condition. Cooling trains, engineering identities, remote-access intermediaries, the directory trust and time dependency belong in the consequence/architecture model. D1 can be outside direct test authority while remaining inside the dependency model. Request its configuration and operating evidence from its owner; do not test it merely because it influences OT.

The passive collection authorization does not permit ARP discovery, a ping sweep or a scanner's discovery phase. Confirm that the collection interface does not transmit and that health monitoring and an independent stop communication are available. The operator can halt the capture, but that does not transfer the facility director's risk-acceptance role to the operator. A final decision should state residual scenarios, evidence uncertainty, treatment prerequisites and the exact configuration/version to which acceptance applies. Summer load is a condition affecting consequence and available recovery time, so it belongs in the assumptions rather than being discarded as a scheduling detail.

guided_practice.prompt: A vendor offers a read-only cloud dashboard but its connector can also upload controller firmware. Amend the charter in four concrete places.
guided_practice.hint: Separate the advertised user interface from the connector privileges and update the boundaries and collection authorization.
guided_practice.solution: Add the connector, cloud tenant and firmware trust path to the architecture; obtain the cloud/vendor ownership and identity evidence route; include unauthorized or corrupted firmware in the scenario scope; define authorized review of connector permissions and update workflow. Do not authorize live firmware transfer implicitly. Revisit the decision criteria and recovery assumptions if the connector changes availability risk.

independent_task.brief: Write a two-page charter for a remote-access review of an EPMS environment. Include an explicit outside-owner dependency and a safe collection plan.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Decision, system boundary, activity authority and consequence boundary are distinct.
At least three measurable stop conditions or collection restrictions are specified.
Residual-risk acceptance belongs to a named accountable owner and has an expiry or change trigger.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Finding the real system boundary and its dependencies
lessons.body:
A subnet is an addressing construct, not a reliable system boundary. An EPMS application can depend on switches in one network, meters in another, a serial gateway, an identity provider, a hypervisor cluster, storage, a time source and a backup repository. A power or cooling function adds non-network dependencies such as shared UPS supply, common pipework and environmental conditions. Start from the required process function and trace the components and services necessary to deliver it.

Use four related views. The physical view locates cabinets, devices, cables, power feeds and physical access. The logical view shows addresses, VLANs, routing, protocol endpoints and application sessions. The administrative view identifies who controls accounts, configurations, keys, updates and supplier services. The process view explains what measurements and commands mean and what happens when they are late, missing or wrong. Reconcile these views using stable identifiers; do not infer physical separation solely from different VLAN colors.

Walk an important transaction end to end. For an operator opening a breaker, identify the operator identity, HMI session, application authorization, command protocol, gateway translation, controller logic, field output and feedback proving final position. Include return traffic and failure indications. A firewall diagram showing only the command direction can hide necessary acknowledgments or an unrestricted alternate route. A historian read path can carry risk through its credentials, software updates or bidirectional connector even if its business purpose is observation.

Create dependency edges with direction and semantics: HMI authenticates to directory; historian reads gateway; gateway polls serial meters; controller depends on time for sequence-of-events labeling. Different semantics imply different failure consequences. Loss of time synchronization may invalidate event ordering while local control continues. Loss of a license server may affect restart but not an already running process. A generic 'connected to' edge obscures these distinctions. Mark whether a dependency is required continuously, at startup, during maintenance or only during recovery.

Redundancy must be analyzed as a dependency graph. Two application servers on the same hypervisor datastore may survive an application crash but fail together after datastore loss. Separate network uplinks can share a conduit, switch chassis, control plane or UPS. Distinguish independent component failures from common-cause events and administrative compromise. A shared privileged account can defeat nominal physical independence. Identify the minimum combinations of failures that interrupt the required function, then confirm that the assumed independence is real.

Reconcile conflicting evidence rather than choosing the neatest drawing. A switch forwarding table shows observed MAC locations but can omit silent devices and show downstream switches behind a trunk. ARP entries connect IP and MAC information only for a recent observation and can be stale. A routing table describes reachability decisions, not application authorization. A firewall configuration shows intended enforcement but needs route and traffic evidence to determine whether the path actually crosses it. Record each source's timestamp and observation limits.

Treat undocumented links as findings requiring controlled investigation. A second HMI NIC might provide a legitimate isolated maintenance path or accidentally route corporate traffic into OT. An unmanaged switch in a cabinet might connect a service laptop and wireless bridge. Document the facts, ownership and uncertainty before concluding maliciousness. The resulting boundary diagram should show external services and trust transitions explicitly, including those outside the test authorization. This model is the foundation for asset criticality, attack paths, zones and conduits, and recovery planning.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC TOPOLOGY FACTS: HMI-A and HMI-B are VMs on hosts HV1 and HV2. Both use datastore DS1 and directory D1. HV1 and HV2 are powered by UPS-U. HMI-A has NIC1 in OT VLAN 120 and NIC2 in corporate VLAN 20; its forwarding setting is unknown. Gateway G1 at 10.120.0.40 polls eight serial meters. Firewall F1 is shown between corporate and OT. A vendor LTE router is cabled to the maintenance switch but absent from the drawing. Local meter displays remain available without G1. Sequence-of-events timestamps use N1.
worked_examples.solution:
The two HMI VMs provide some host-level resilience but share DS1, D1 and UPS-U. Their service availability is therefore conditional on those shared resources and on whether cached sessions or local credentials support degraded operation. G1 aggregates eight meter communication paths; its loss removes remote visibility to those meters but does not erase their local displays. The risk consequence must state this distinction.

HMI-A's second NIC and the LTE router are candidate alternate trust paths. The supplied evidence does not prove that HMI-A forwards traffic or that the router is active. Obtain interface, route, forwarding and service-binding information through authorized methods, inspect the physical connection and ask for the LTE service owner. F1 cannot be credited as the sole corporate/OT boundary until alternate routes are resolved. N1 loss primarily changes the trustworthiness of event ordering in the supplied facts; it is not evidence that every breaker loses local protection. The boundary diagram should connect each dependency to the function affected and identify which facts still require verification.

guided_practice.prompt: Add a backup server that is reachable only through D1 authentication and stores backups on DS1. Identify two ways the recovery claim can fail.
guided_practice.hint: Trace the recovery workflow after loss of the services on which that workflow depends.
guided_practice.solution: Loss of DS1 can remove both production disks and the colocated backup copies. Loss or compromise of D1 can prevent authorized recovery access or authorize destructive access to both copies. Verify independent storage, recovery credentials and an offline or otherwise independently protected restoration route.

independent_task.brief: Produce four synchronized views of the supplied EPMS topology, then add one documented common-cause failure and one unresolved alternate access path.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Every dependency edge has direction, purpose and operating phase.
The diagrams distinguish known connections from hypotheses.
Redundancy claims name shared resources and the specific failures tolerated.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Asset identity, firmware applicability and evidence provenance
lessons.body:
An asset inventory is an evidence model, not merely a spreadsheet of addresses. The minimum useful record connects a physical or virtual item to its function, owner, location, communication interfaces, software/firmware baseline, support status, critical dependencies and the provenance of those facts. Select an identifier that survives routine IP changes. A manufacturer serial number combined with site identity can distinguish physical devices; a managed VM UUID plus an application identifier can distinguish virtual instances. Neither MAC nor hostname is universally permanent or unique.

Separate the installed baseline from a catalog description. A product family can contain different hardware revisions, optional communication modules, operating systems and firmware branches. Vulnerability applicability often depends on the exact affected component, version interval, enabled feature and reachable interface. Record controller firmware and network-module firmware separately when the product architecture separates them. A scanner banner may describe a proxy, embedded web server or gateway rather than the process controller behind it.

Use evidence sources according to their strengths. Procurement records establish what was purchased, not necessarily what is installed. Engineering project files describe intended configuration and may be stale. A signed owner export provides a current configuration snapshot if the source and time are established. Passive traffic identifies observed behavior and endpoints but misses powered-off, silent and non-network components. A physical walkdown can identify a cabinet and serial label but should not involve removing covers or entering energized equipment without the necessary authorization and qualified personnel. Combine sources and record conflicts explicitly.

Track observation time, collection method, collector, source file identifier and integrity digest where evidence must remain reproducible. A hash can show that an exported file has not changed since hashing; it does not prove the original export was accurate or that the source device was uncompromised. Protect inventories because addresses, firmware versions and trust relationships can aid an attacker. Apply access control, retention and secure sharing appropriate to the assessment, while ensuring the owner can maintain the record after the consultant leaves.

Confidence labels should describe what is known. 'Confirmed from current device export' differs from 'inferred from passive banner' and 'reported by owner, not verified'. Do not convert a missing version into 'latest'. Maintain an unresolved-evidence queue with owner and due date. Where an unsupported asset cannot be queried safely, document the reason and use an approved alternative such as an existing maintenance record or an offline image from a spare. The inability to collect one field is a limitation, not authority to increase collection risk.

Model identities and software as assets too. Service accounts, certificates, trust anchors, automation scripts, engineering project files, golden images and backup sets can authorize or reproduce process-affecting behavior. Link a service account to its application, privileges, credential storage and rotation process; an account name alone does not reveal effective access. Link backup artifacts to the precise devices and software they can restore. A recoverable configuration without its required license, firmware or project password may not constitute a recoverable service.

Deduplicate carefully. The same physical controller can appear under multiple addresses, while two devices can reuse a factory-default hostname. Preserve interface-level records beneath the asset record. Reconcile replacement history: a new device using the old IP is a different hardware instance and may have a different trust state. Inventory maintenance should be coupled to commissioning, replacement, firmware change, account creation and decommissioning. This makes the assessment baseline sustainable and allows vulnerability notices to be matched to actual deployed conditions.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — INVENTORY EXTRACT (synthetic): Row A: IP 10.120.0.40, hostname GW-DEFAULT, serial G-771, gateway OS 4.2.1 from signed export dated 2026-09-10, protocol module 2.8 from device export. Row B: IP 10.120.0.41, hostname GW-DEFAULT, serial G-772, version unknown, inferred model from a passive HTTP banner. Row C: IP 10.120.0.40, serial G-771, firmware 3.9 from procurement spreadsheet dated 2023. Advisory V-17 affects protocol module 2.7 through 2.9 only when remote write service is enabled. A's write-service status is not yet collected. B was replaced last month but retained its IP. Account svc_epms can read meters and administer G1 according to an owner statement not yet verified.
worked_examples.solution:
Rows A and C describe the same serial G-771 and should be reconciled into one asset with conflicting historical evidence, not counted as two gateways. The current device export is stronger evidence of the installed gateway OS than the older purchasing record, while the purchasing record remains useful for history. Gateway OS 4.2.1 does not answer whether V-17 affects the protocol module: module 2.8 falls in the stated affected range, but the enabled write-service condition remains unresolved. Report conditional applicability and obtain the feature configuration through an authorized read-only export.

Row B must remain a separate physical asset despite sharing the default hostname. Its recent replacement means older version evidence tied only to the IP can be wrong. Establish the new serial, hardware revision and current firmware. For svc_epms, split the intended meter-read role from the claimed gateway-administration capability and obtain effective permission evidence. A service with administrative capability is not safely characterized as a read-only collection account. Record each conclusion's source and confidence rather than silently upgrading owner statements into verified facts.

guided_practice.prompt: A network scan reports version 5.0 for an address whose cabinet label identifies a serial controller. Give a verification sequence that avoids an unsupported vulnerability conclusion.
guided_practice.hint: Identify which device terminates the scanned service and distinguish gateway software from downstream controller firmware.
guided_practice.solution: Reconcile the IP/MAC/switch attachment to the gateway; identify the service and component that emitted the banner; compare it with a current approved configuration or version export; obtain downstream controller information through its documented engineering records or authorized interface; map the advisory to the exact affected component and enabled feature before assigning applicability.

independent_task.brief: Create an inventory schema and reconcile the supplied rows while retaining conflicting evidence and a queue of missing facts.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Stable device identity is distinct from interfaces and reused addresses.
OS and protocol-module versions are not conflated.
Every conclusion retains source date, collection method and confidence.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Process hazards, consequence timing and cyber criticality
lessons.body:
Process hazard analysis explains how departures from intended process behavior can cause harm. It may describe deviations such as no flow, high pressure, reverse flow, excessive temperature or incorrect sequence; initiating conditions; safeguards; and consequences. A cybersecurity assessment uses this engineering knowledge to ask whether digital actions can create, conceal or prolong those deviations. It does not replace the qualified safety team's hazard study, validate a safety instrumented function by inspection of a network diagram, or convert a cybersecurity rating into a safety integrity level.

Begin with the physical function and its acceptable operating envelope. Identify controlled variables, manipulated variables, sensors, actuators, interlocks and operator actions. For cooling, the relevant mechanism may be loss of flow, an incorrect valve position, a false low-temperature reading or a disabled alarm. Distinguish loss of a measurement from a believable incorrect measurement. A controller may handle a missing sensor with an alarm and fallback, while accepting a plausible but false reading that drives the process in the wrong direction. Integrity scenarios therefore require more than availability analysis.

Translate each proposed digital action into a causal chain. For example: an unauthorized engineering session changes a high-temperature alarm threshold; the HMI continues showing apparently normal values; operators do not initiate load reduction; the cooling shortfall persists; equipment exceeds its approved envelope. Each arrow needs a technical or operational justification. Do not leap from 'open TCP port' directly to 'catastrophic outage' without showing the vulnerable function, attacker capability, process effect and protective responses. Conversely, do not dismiss a low-bandwidth link because its few bytes can carry a high-consequence command.

Time is often the decisive constraint. Compare detection, communication, diagnosis, authorization and action times with the process time available before an unacceptable state. Use consistent units and identify whether activities overlap or occur sequentially. A nominal five-minute operator response is inadequate when the required workflow includes a separate three-minute diagnosis and a four-minute authorization, unless the claimed five minutes already includes them. Use conservative validated bounds where necessary, and label a calculation based on assumed times as a scenario estimate rather than a measured guarantee.

Evaluate safeguards for the specific scenario. A hardwired protective trip may be independent of a compromised HMI, but only if its sensors, logic, power and final elements do not share the compromised path in a way that defeats the protection. A second screen displaying the same data source is not an independent measurement. A manual procedure requires available people, access, authority, correct information and time. A safety system's certified component rating does not automatically establish that the integrated installation remains effective under the cyber scenario being analyzed.

Cyber criticality belongs to functions and dependencies as well as devices. A historian may not control the process directly but can be critical to incident reconstruction, regulatory records or detection of slow manipulation. A time server may be essential for trustworthy event ordering yet unnecessary for local protective action. State which consequence dimension gives an asset its criticality. This avoids classifying every networked device as equally critical and helps select appropriate assessment depth and controls.

Keep consequence severity separate from how likely the scenario is. Severe outcomes can be physically possible but require multiple conditions; likelihood analysis evaluates those conditions later. Record whether an outcome is credible given plant configuration, operating mode, safeguards and duration. Use existing hazard studies as evidence and involve their owners when cyber assumptions expose gaps. The output should be a scenario-to-process map with safe operating limits, causal links, credited protections, response-time assumptions and unresolved validation needs.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — COOLING SCENARIO (synthetic): At the assessed load, loss of both cooling trains gives an estimated 12 minutes before the approved inlet-temperature envelope is exceeded. An HMI alarm normally appears 2 minutes after loss of flow. Operator diagnosis takes 3 minutes, authorization 2 minutes and load shedding 4 minutes, sequentially after the alarm. A separate hardwired high-temperature trip acts at 10 minutes, but it shares the same sensor power supply as the compromised controller. Two HMI screens read the same controller value. The hazard study describes overheating consequences; its independence assumptions have not been reviewed for malicious sensor-power loss.
worked_examples.solution:
The manual response path totals 2 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 11 minutes from loss of flow, leaving only one minute against the estimated 12-minute envelope. This narrow nominal margin does not establish robust performance: the study must consider uncertainty, missed alarms, staffing and the operating conditions used to derive the 12-minute estimate. If the attack suppresses the HMI alarm, the two-minute detection assumption is invalid and the manual path may not start.

The hardwired trip cannot automatically receive independent-protection credit against sensor-power compromise because it shares that supply. The two HMI displays likewise do not provide independent measurement integrity. Ask the safety and controls teams to validate the relevant failure behavior, power arrangement and process response in an authorized representative environment. Keep the overheating consequence and possible safety implications visible without asserting a SIL determination. The cyber assessment identifies how an adversarial condition challenges the hazard study's assumptions and what evidence is required to resolve that challenge.

guided_practice.prompt: An independent detector alarms at minute 5 and operators can shed load in 6 minutes after that alarm. Calculate the nominal margin, then name two reasons it may not be adequate.
guided_practice.hint: Use the 12-minute envelope and distinguish a numerical margin from validated reliability.
guided_practice.solution: The path is 5 + 6 = 11 minutes, leaving one minute. Detector timing and operator-action variability could consume the margin; the 12-minute thermal estimate may shorten at higher load or degraded cooling. Verify independence, event detection coverage and bounded response time rather than treating the arithmetic as proof of safety.

lessons.title: Threat scenarios, adversary capability and attack paths
lessons.body:
A threat scenario is a specific account of how an event can exploit or interact with system conditions to produce an adverse outcome. It should identify the threat source or event, starting access, relevant capability and intent where applicable, enabling vulnerabilities or predisposing conditions, the sequence of actions, affected functions, existing safeguards and resulting consequences. Use this structure for malicious actors, accidental misuse and environmental or equipment events where they contribute to cyber-related risk. Do not use an adversary label as a substitute for a technical path.

Starting access matters. An internet attacker, a compromised vendor laptop, an authenticated but overprivileged technician and an engineer already inside the maintenance zone begin with different opportunities. An internet-facing login service does not mean the actor can directly issue a controller command. Conversely, a legacy controller without individual authentication may place most of its security burden on upstream access control and physical restrictions. State the assumed foothold explicitly so that likelihood and treatment discussions do not drift between incompatible scenarios.

Separate authentication, authorization and process capability. A stolen password may allow login but not administration if an independent second factor and role restrictions are enforced. An authenticated engineering account may legitimately hold process-affecting privileges whose misuse must be controlled through approval, time limitation and monitoring. A compromised monitoring server can be dangerous even if its normal application performs reads, because stored credentials or a management interface may provide write capability. Follow effective privileges and trust relationships, not only normal traffic purpose.

Construct an attack path as a sequence of prerequisites and transitions. For each transition, ask what access is required, which service or trust decision is crossed, what evidence establishes feasibility, and what control would block or detect it. Paths can branch: a vendor account may reach either a jump host or an unmanaged alternate tunnel. Paths can combine conditions: a harmful change may require both an engineering session and a disabled interlock. Distinguish AND conditions from alternative OR paths. Counting five controls along one path is misleading if one alternate path bypasses all five.

Avoid false precision about capability. If the scenario assumes a stolen legitimate credential and an allowed engineering workflow, it may not require a novel software exploit. If it assumes bypassing a hardened cryptographic device, substantial additional capability and evidence are needed. Describe the work the actor must accomplish rather than assigning a dramatic actor category. Record intent only where it matters to the outcome; accidental selection of the wrong project can produce a similar process change through a different initiating event and likelihood model.

Threat modeling should include integrity, availability and misuse of authorized functions. Examples include delayed telemetry that remains marked good, altered alarm limits, unauthorized firmware, replayed commands, denial of remote visibility, compromised recovery images and destruction of engineering project files. Map each to the affected process or evidence function. A threat list becomes useful when it identifies where to collect evidence and which controls the design must implement.

Maintain clear evidence status. A demonstrated authorized path in a representative lab is different from a hypothesized path inferred from a diagram. Absence of an exploit demonstration does not prove safety, and a laboratory demonstration does not establish that every production condition matches. Use bounded analytical reasoning where live testing would be inappropriate. The resulting scenario record should be understandable to controls, network, safety and operations personnel, with assumptions and alternative paths visible enough for them to challenge.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — REMOTE MAINTENANCE CASE (synthetic): Vendor user V logs into gateway R with password plus MFA. R permits V to jump host J during an approved two-hour window. J stores a shared engineering credential E that can modify controller setpoints. Session recording is enabled on R. Controller C accepts E from J and also from maintenance laptop L on the local switch. L has an unmanaged cellular connection. A proposed scenario begins with theft of V's password alone. A second begins with compromise of an already authenticated J session. The interlock preventing operation outside the approved range is local to C and its independence is not yet verified.
worked_examples.solution:
Password theft alone does not complete the path through R if MFA is effectively enforced and the attacker lacks the second factor or a session-bypass mechanism. That scenario needs an additional transition rather than an assumed immediate controller takeover. Compromise of an already authenticated J session starts farther along the path and can expose E or its authorized engineering functions. Session recording may support detection and reconstruction, but it does not by itself prevent a harmful setpoint write.

L creates an alternate route to C that may bypass R's MFA, time window and recording. Evaluate that path with its own starting access and controls. The local interlock can constrain process consequences only if its behavior and independence hold under the proposed manipulation. Do not assume that a write automatically defeats the interlock or that the interlock is adequate merely because it exists. A useful scenario graph therefore separates access to R, access to J, use of E, access through L, setpoint modification and the conditions required for an unacceptable physical outcome.

guided_practice.prompt: Write separate scenarios for accidental wrong-project download and malicious use of E. Identify one shared treatment and one treatment specific to the initiating event.
guided_practice.hint: Both may use legitimate engineering privileges, but intent, detection opportunities and preventive workflow differ.
guided_practice.solution: Both benefit from independently checked configuration identity, bounded privileges, recoverable approved baselines and validation of process constraints. Accidental wrong-project download additionally benefits from clear asset/project matching and an error-resistant approval workflow; malicious credential misuse requires strong identity/session protection, restricted paths and detection of suspicious authorized-function use. Do not infer equal likelihood merely because the final command is similar.

independent_task.brief: Create an attack-path graph for the supplied remote-maintenance case with at least two starting access conditions and one AND condition governing the physical consequence.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Each edge names a capability or trust transition supported by facts or labeled assumptions.
The cellular alternate path is analyzed separately from R.
Detection controls are not credited as automatic prevention.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Passive network evidence and protocol interpretation
lessons.body:
Passive collection observes traffic without intentionally interrogating the monitored devices. It can reveal peers, protocols, timing, unexpected write operations, retransmissions and communication changes. It cannot prove that every installed device was observed, that an unobserved service is disabled, or that an observed message was authorized by the process owner. The collection architecture itself must be approved: a mirror destination may still transmit if the attached interface is misconfigured, and switch mirroring can consume resources or drop mirrored packets under load.

Document where the capture is taken. A mirror of one access port sees a different set of transactions from a mirror of a trunk or a routed boundary. Specify directions, VLAN handling, timestamp source, truncation length and the capture interval. If ingress and egress copies of the same traffic are both mirrored, duplicate packets can appear. If the mirror destination is oversubscribed, missing frames may reflect observation loss rather than loss on the production link. Collector drop counters and switch mirror limitations therefore belong with the packet evidence.

Interpret layers in order. Ethernet source and destination identify the local frame delivery context, which may change at a router. IP addresses identify network-layer endpoints or translated addresses. TCP sequence and acknowledgment behavior describes stream delivery, not application authorization. Application fields describe the requested operation. In a synthetic Modbus TCP example, function 3 reads holding registers, function 6 writes one holding register, and function 16 writes multiple holding registers. Register addresses are offsets in the protocol data unit; a vendor document's human-facing register numbering may add a convention such as a 40001 base. Confirm the product map and units before interpreting a value as a temperature or command.

A protocol operation's meaning depends on the process and device implementation. A write to a register might set a harmless display parameter, change an alarm limit, reset a counter or command an actuator. An exception response indicates the request was rejected at the application level, but its cause needs interpretation. For example, an illegal data address response suggests the requested register is not accepted in that context; it does not by itself prove an intrusion prevention system blocked an attacker. A successful TCP connection likewise does not prove a successful process command.

Distinguish repeated application requests from transport retransmission. TCP may retransmit bytes because an acknowledgment was not observed, while the application may also issue a new transaction with a new identifier. A capture missing one direction can make normal sessions appear incomplete. Compare sequence numbers, transaction identifiers, timestamps and response content before counting events. Where a protocol operation is not safely idempotent, repeated execution can matter; the assessment should establish the device's duplicate-handling and application retry behavior using documentation or a representative authorized test.

Encrypted traffic changes the evidence available. A passive observer may see endpoint relationships, certificate exchange where exposed, timing and volume while being unable to inspect the protected application commands. Encryption is not evidence of benign intent, and inability to decode does not justify claiming that no writes occurred. Correlate approved gateway, application and controller audit logs with the capture, maintaining time-quality uncertainty. A packet timestamp from an unsynchronized collector cannot support precise event ordering across unrelated systems without adjustment.

Turn observations into bounded findings. State what was observed, where, when, under which capture conditions and with what confidence. Compare it with the approved communication matrix and maintenance schedule. A write outside an approved window is a concrete discrepancy to investigate, not automatic proof of malicious intent. Preserve the original capture and a reproducible filter or event extraction so a second analyst can examine the same evidence. Use synthetic traces here; actual collection requires owner authorization and appropriate handling of operational data.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC DECODED TRACE; no real packet capture was executed. Mirror: S1 uplink, both directions; collector reports 4% dropped packets during a burst. Approved policy: H=10.120.0.10 reads G=10.120.0.40; engineering writes allowed from J=10.120.0.20 only 13:00–14:00 UTC. Events: 12:58:00 H→G TCP/502 transaction 91 function 3 start offset 100 count 2; G→H normal response. 12:59:10 J→G transaction 92 function 6 offset 110 value 750; G→J normal echo. 12:59:10.2 J→G same TCP sequence and transaction 92 observed again. 13:05:00 H→G transaction 93 function 16 offset 200 count 2; G→H exception code 2. Device map: offset 110 is high-temperature alarm threshold in 0.1°C; offsets 200–201 are not writable in this operating mode. Collector clock is 90 seconds ahead of trusted UTC.
worked_examples.solution:
The function-6 write requests an alarm threshold of 75.0°C according to the supplied map; do not infer a universal meaning for register 110 on other devices. Correcting the collector's 90-second lead places the write at 12:57:40 UTC, outside the approved 13:00–14:00 window. The normal echo supports application-level acceptance of that write request, although a separate readback or device audit record is needed to establish persistent configuration and any physical effect.

The repeated transaction with the same TCP sequence is consistent with transport retransmission or duplicate mirror observation, not necessarily a second independently issued engineering action. The 4% collector-drop condition weakens claims about completeness and can explain missing acknowledgments. The function-16 request from H is an unexpected write-capable operation by a read-designated source, but exception code 2 and the device map indicate rejection of that address in this mode. Investigate the client configuration and authorization without reporting that the two registers were successfully changed. Retain corrected and original timestamps and document the clock-offset evidence.

guided_practice.prompt: A capture shows an encrypted session from J to a gateway during the maintenance window and no visible Modbus writes. State what can and cannot be concluded, then identify corroborating evidence.
guided_practice.hint: Encrypted application content is not the same as absent application operations.
guided_practice.solution: The capture supports the existence and timing of the encrypted endpoint relationship within its observation limits. It does not establish which engineering commands traversed the session or whether they were authorized. Correlate gateway session logs, named user identity, approved change records, controller audit/readback and trustworthy time sources.

independent_task.brief: Analyze the supplied trace into an event table with original and corrected times, operation meaning, policy comparison and evidence limitations.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Register values use the supplied units and map.
Rejected operations, accepted requests and confirmed physical effects are distinguished.
Capture drops and duplicate observations are reflected in confidence.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Active assessment design, safety limits and representative testing
lessons.body:
Active assessment sends traffic or invokes functions to learn about a system. Discovery probes, authenticated configuration queries, vulnerability checks and penetration tests have different interaction depth, but none is intrinsically harmless merely because a tool labels it safe or read-only. Embedded devices can fail under unexpected connections, malformed requests, session exhaustion or rates that ordinary servers tolerate. An authenticated inventory query can still trigger expensive processing, logs, lockouts or fragile legacy services. Method selection must follow the operational decision and evidence need.

Start with the least intrusive method that can answer the question. Existing configuration exports, vendor advisories and passive observations may establish enough information to determine an exposed service or affected version. When active confirmation adds necessary value, define the exact uncertainty it will resolve. 'Run the scanner' is not a test objective. A useful objective might be to confirm that a specified management service is reachable only from the maintenance zone, using a bounded connection attempt that does not authenticate or alter process state.

Prepare an approved rules-of-engagement record. Identify exact target addresses and stable assets, source interfaces, route restrictions, approved checks, excluded plugins, credentials and privilege, request rates, concurrency, time window, operator oversight, health indicators, stop authority and communication. Include what happens if a target address resolves to a replacement or an unexpected device. Freeze the tool version and relevant configuration so the assessed behavior can be reproduced; an automatic plugin update can change what a named scan profile actually does.

Use representative testing before touching sensitive assets. A spare with matching hardware, firmware, enabled services and configuration can reveal failure modes, although it may not reproduce production load, network dependencies or process coupling. Record the differences and avoid treating a spare's success as universal proof. A virtual appliance may emulate a gateway's IP services while omitting serial timing, physical I/O and watchdog behavior. The validation environment should be chosen for the specific risk the test could introduce.

Set quantitative limits from validated behavior and owner constraints, not from a generic universal threshold. Concurrency can matter independently of packet rate: a low-rate test that holds many sessions open can exhaust a connection table. A short malformed request can be more disruptive than many normal reads. Separate the scan's discovery phase from its vulnerability plugins; disabling aggressive plugins does not necessarily disable discovery traffic or broadcast probes. Validate source binding and target allowlists before execution so a second laptop interface cannot route tests onto an unintended segment.

Define stop criteria that can be observed promptly. Examples include a process alarm, communication watchdog change, target CPU or session count exceeding an approved bound, unexpected controller mode transition, rising response latency, loss of operator visibility or a mismatch between expected and actual target identity. Specify who watches each indicator and how the test is halted. Stopping the tool may not restore a hung service, so the restoration plan must include authorized recovery actions, required backups, support contacts and criteria for verifying normal operation.

Distinguish assessment from exploitation. A vulnerability assessment identifies and evaluates weaknesses; a penetration test demonstrates selected attack paths under explicit authorization and constraints. A production owner may decline exploitation while allowing offline validation on a representative device. That limit should be reported honestly without implying the system is secure. Findings should include method, coverage, untested conditions, evidence and applicability. Do not hide a disrupted asset or a stopped test as a successful clean result; the operational observation itself is relevant evidence.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — APPROVED TEST PLAN DRAFT (synthetic; no scanner is run): Target spare gateway S matches production gateway P's model and protocol firmware 2.8, but S has no serial devices attached. Proposed production test: source laptop interface eth0; P at 10.120.0.40; maximum two concurrent TCP sessions; only an approved management-service connection check; 02:00–02:10 window. Excluded: login attempts, malformed packets, write functions and broadcast discovery. Stop if polling p95 latency exceeds 120 ms for 30 seconds, a watchdog alarm occurs, or target identity differs. Normal polling p95 is 45 ms. A scanner profile auto-enables discovery and downloads plugin updates at launch. The laptop also has Wi-Fi connected to corporate IT. Recovery instructions mention reboot but contain no approved process coordination or verified configuration backup.
worked_examples.solution:
The named scanner profile is not yet compatible with the approved plan: automatic discovery may transmit excluded probes, and updated plugins make the behavior different from the version reviewed. Freeze and inspect the actual checks, disable excluded discovery, verify target allowlisting and bind the approved source path. Corporate Wi-Fi introduces an unintended route and must be handled according to the approved collection design rather than ignored.

The spare provides some evidence about the same protocol firmware, but the absent serial load means it does not validate production polling latency or gateway behavior under real serial transactions. The 120 ms/30-second criterion is a case-specific approved bound, not a generally safe OT threshold. Reboot is not a complete recovery plan; determine process impact, authorized operator coordination, current configuration restoration and normal-state checks first. Until these gaps are resolved, the plan is not ready for the proposed production test. An assessment can document that limitation without inventing test results.

guided_practice.prompt: An assessor reduces packet rate but opens fifty persistent sessions. Explain why this can still violate a two-session approved limit and affect availability.
guided_practice.hint: Rate and concurrent resource occupancy are different quantities.
guided_practice.solution: Fifty simultaneous sessions exceed the explicit limit even if new packets arrive slowly. Each session can consume memory, sockets or application slots; retained sessions can exhaust resources while packet rate remains low. Constrain concurrency and lifetime as well as request rate, then verify cleanup and normal polling behavior in the representative environment.

independent_task.brief: Rewrite the draft into a test-ready plan for an isolated representative gateway. Keep production execution outside this exercise.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The uncertainty to resolve and the exact permitted interactions are explicit.
Tool version, discovery behavior, targets and source routing are controlled.
Stop, restoration and normal-operation acceptance criteria are actionable.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Vulnerability research, applicability and false-positive resolution
lessons.body:
A vulnerability record describes a weakness under specified conditions. The assessment must determine whether those conditions exist in the installed system and whether the weakness contributes to a relevant threat scenario. Begin with the supplier's advisory and affected-product table, then corroborate identifiers and technical details through authoritative vulnerability sources where available. Keep the advisory revision date because affected ranges, mitigations and fixed versions can change after publication. A search result snippet or scanner plugin title is not a complete applicability analysis.

Match the exact component, hardware variant, software branch and enabled feature. Version comparison is often product-specific: 2.10 is ordinarily a later minor version than 2.9, not a decimal value smaller than 2.9. Build metadata and hotfix identifiers may matter, and a vendor may backport a fix without changing the upstream component version exposed in a banner. Use the supplier's release documentation and installed package/build evidence before declaring a patched system vulnerable or an unpatched branch fixed. Never infer support solely from a version number that looks recent.

Distinguish four questions. Is affected code present? Is the vulnerable function enabled and reachable under the scenario's starting access? Can the required action be performed with the actor's capability? What process or service consequence follows if the weakness is exercised? A firewall can reduce reachability without removing the code flaw. Disabling a feature may remove the relevant exposure while leaving the device on an affected software version. A patch can remove one weakness while introducing compatibility or availability concerns requiring validation. Record these as different treatment and evidence states.

Scanner results are leads, not unquestionable verdicts. A banner-based check may flag a vulnerable version even when a documented fix is backported. An authenticated check may inspect a package but miss a separately installed protocol module. A network check may see a reverse proxy's version while the advisory applies to the backend. False-negative risk also matters: a scanner can miss an unreachable management interface that becomes available during maintenance, or omit a proprietary function it cannot identify. Record method and coverage, and resolve disputed findings with component-specific evidence.

A generic severity score supports prioritization but is not the site's risk result. It may describe technical exploit conditions and generic impacts without representing the cooling or power process, shared safeguards, operating mode, recovery time or local consequence criteria. A high-scoring vulnerability on an isolated spare may be less urgent operationally than a lower-scoring weakness that permits a critical alarm limit to be altered through an exposed engineering workflow. This does not justify ignoring severe vulnerabilities; it requires explaining the local scenario and residual exposure rather than copying the score into a risk matrix.

Exploit availability affects some likelihood judgments but must be interpreted carefully. A public proof of concept may demonstrate only a crash on a particular build, not reliable code execution on the installed platform. Absence of a public exploit does not prove that no actor can exploit the weakness. Indicators of active exploitation can increase urgency when the installed conditions match, but do not remove the need to identify asset applicability. Record intelligence source, date and confidence, and avoid claiming a live compromise from vulnerability presence alone.

The finding record should contain the affected asset and component, evidence baseline, advisory revision, applicability conditions, observed or inferred exposure, potential scenario, current safeguards, uncertainty, treatment options, owner and validation plan. If a fix cannot yet be applied, document the compensating controls and their failure modes, time limit and review trigger. A closure claim should identify what changed and how that change was verified; 'patch planned' is not 'remediated', and 'port filtered from one source' is not 'affected code removed'.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — ADVISORY TRIAGE (synthetic identifiers, not real CVEs): VA-21 affects gateway protocol module versions 2.7 through 2.9 inclusive when remote write service is enabled; fixed branch is 2.10 or vendor hotfix HF-21 for 2.8. Asset A runs module 2.8 with verified HF-21 and remote write enabled. Asset B runs 2.9 with write disabled in a current export. Asset C runs 2.10; a scanner compares versions as decimal numbers and flags it. Asset D runs 2.8 with write enabled; firewall allows only jump host J, whose engineering session is in the threat scope. The generic advisory severity is high. A public demonstration crashes an unpatched lab gateway; it does not demonstrate code execution. The supplier requires compatibility validation before production upgrade.
worked_examples.solution:
A has affected-looking base version metadata but also verified vendor HF-21, so the advisory's documented hotfix route is material evidence of remediation. Confirm the hotfix applies to the exact component and preserve the installation evidence. B retains affected code but the stated vulnerable feature is disabled; classify the scenario as mitigated or not exposed under that configuration, with a trigger if remote write is enabled. Do not call B patched.

C is in the stated fixed branch. The scanner's decimal comparison is a false-positive mechanism because dotted software versions are not decimal fractions. D remains relevant despite the firewall because J is an allowed source and a compromised engineering session is explicitly within scope. The lab crash demonstration supports an availability effect on its tested build, not arbitrary code execution or a confirmed production incident. Select treatment using the site's consequences and constraints, then validate the patch or compensating control against the actual scenario and approved operational requirements.

guided_practice.prompt: A vendor advisory revision expands the affected range to include one hardware variant previously excluded. Describe the reassessment steps.
guided_practice.hint: Use stable asset identity and retained advisory/version provenance to find the affected assumptions.
guided_practice.solution: Compare the revised hardware and component conditions with the inventory, identify previously excluded findings and their owners, refresh exposure and consequence analysis for matching assets, review existing acceptance decisions and compensating controls, prioritize treatment with current operational constraints, and retain both advisory revisions so the changed conclusion is traceable.

independent_task.brief: Produce an applicability table for A–D with separate columns for affected code, vulnerable feature, reachable path, remediation state and evidence confidence.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Hotfix evidence and version ordering are interpreted correctly.
Filtered, disabled, patched and unknown are not collapsed into one status.
Local risk reasoning adds process context beyond generic severity.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Windows engineering stations and application-host assessment
lessons.body:
Engineering workstations and application servers connect general-purpose computing to process-affecting functions. Their assessment must examine both the operating system and the engineering application. A supported OS with an overprivileged project-download tool can still expose a critical control path; a hardened host without a compatible recovery image can become an availability liability. Identify the host's role, required software, hardware interfaces, controller protocols, domain dependencies and authorized maintenance workflows before judging individual settings.

Use current authorized exports and approved native read-only inspection in a representative environment. For a Windows Server 2019 or Windows 10-based example, PowerShell commands such as Get-SmbServerConfiguration, Get-LocalGroupMember and Get-CimInstance Win32_Service can expose relevant configuration when run with suitable authorization and privileges. These are illustrative command names, not commands executed by this programme; actual platform editions, PowerShell versions, domain policies and vendor support must be checked. A single local setting may be overridden or complemented by effective domain policy, application settings and host firewall rules.

Assess services by necessity, binding, authentication, authorization and implementation. An unnecessary file-sharing service increases exposure, but disabling a required engineering repository without understanding dependencies can interrupt operations. Legacy SMB support, absent message signing or broadly writable shares each creates a different concern. Encryption, signing and authentication are distinct: confidentiality protects content from disclosure, integrity protections resist modification, and identity/authorization determine who may perform actions. Do not credit one setting with every property.

Examine effective privilege. Local administrator membership can enable service changes, credential access and application manipulation. A domain group nested into a local group may grant access indirectly, so a short list of local usernames is incomplete evidence. Service accounts should have the rights required by their function and controlled credential storage; a service running as a highly privileged identity may be necessary for a documented vendor function but still creates a consequence that needs compensating controls and validation. Do not change service identities blindly on production engineering software.

Protect the artifacts that define process behavior. Project files, scripts, configuration templates and firmware packages may become an integrity path to controllers even if the host cannot issue an immediate command. Review write permissions, provenance, change approval, version history and the verification performed before download. A backup directory writable by the same compromised service account as the live project is vulnerable to common administrative compromise. Read-only copies, independent retention and verified restore procedures must be evaluated for their actual access controls and failure domains.

Application control and removable-media controls need operational testing. An allowlist can reduce unauthorized execution but may fail open, run only in audit mode, or allow broad writable paths. A rule permitting any executable in a user-writable engineering folder offers weaker protection than an appropriately maintained trusted-signature or exact-artifact policy. Updates and emergency tools require a controlled workflow so operators do not bypass the control permanently. Audit mode provides observations for tuning; it is not equivalent to blocking execution.

Review logs with time, coverage and retention in mind. Security log rollover may erase the relevant engineering session before an incident is recognized. A successful login record does not identify every application command unless the application logs them. Remote log forwarding can improve preservation but depends on network paths, storage and source authenticity. Finally, evaluate recovery with compatible OS, application version, drivers, licenses, projects, certificates and credentials. A clean OS installation alone may not restore the engineering function. Findings should connect each host weakness to a process or recovery scenario and preserve vendor compatibility and change-control constraints.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC WINDOWS HOST EXPORT, Windows Server 2019 example; commands and outputs are illustrative and unexecuted. HMI-SRV: SMB1 enabled=True; SMB signing required=False; local Administrators contains OT-Engineers domain group; membership nesting not collected. Service ProjectSync runs as LocalSystem and reads/writes D:\Projects and D:\Backups. Both folders grant Modify to svc_sync. Application control Mode=AuditOnly; rule allows executables from D:\Projects\Tools, writable by OT-Engineers. Security log MaximumSize=20 MB, overwrite as needed; measured normal rollover is 6 hours. Incident recognition objective is 24 hours. Current recovery folder includes project files but no verified application installer, license recovery procedure or compatible driver package. Vendor supports a tested hardening baseline, not arbitrary service removal.
worked_examples.solution:
The export identifies several distinct issues. SMB1 enabled is a legacy protocol exposure to evaluate against required clients and the supported hardening baseline. Signing not required is an integrity/authentication-session concern separate from whether traffic is encrypted. The Administrators entry requires effective membership analysis because nested domain membership can widen privilege beyond the visible local list.

ProjectSync and svc_sync create two related trust paths: a highly privileged running service and a credential that can modify both active projects and backups. A compromise may alter the process configuration and its restoration source. Application control in audit-only mode does not block execution, and the writable Tools path would need careful rule design even in enforcement mode. Six-hour log rollover is shorter than the 24-hour recognition objective, leaving an evidence gap unless another verified source preserves the records. Recovery is incomplete because project files alone do not establish that the supported engineering application, license and drivers can be restored. Recommend a validated hardening and recovery plan rather than immediately disabling services without dependency analysis.

guided_practice.prompt: An engineer proposes switching application control to enforcement immediately. Identify a representative test and two acceptance criteria.
guided_practice.hint: Consider both unwanted execution and required commissioning or recovery functions.
guided_practice.solution: Use an isolated host matching the supported OS, application, drivers and representative projects. Confirm required engineering, update and recovery workflows operate under the candidate policy; verify an unapproved executable in the writable Tools directory is blocked and logged. Confirm emergency exception handling and rollback before considering an authorized production change.

independent_task.brief: Build a host finding register that separates network service exposure, effective privilege, project integrity, evidence retention and recovery completeness.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Each finding states the relevant host evidence and process or recovery implication.
Audit mode is not credited as preventive enforcement.
Remediation preserves documented vendor compatibility and has a representative validation plan.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Identity chains, privilege concentration and emergency access
lessons.body:
Identity assessment follows the chain from a claimed principal to an effective action. For a remote engineer, the chain may include a federated identity provider, MFA service, access gateway, jump host, application role and controller credential. For a service, it may include a certificate, private key store, application account and downstream device permissions. A strong first login does not automatically constrain every later stage. Draw the chain and record which component authenticates the principal, which authorizes each action and which identity appears in the audit record.

Named accounts improve attribution only when the subsequent workflow preserves the mapping. If every engineer logs into a jump host individually but then uses one shared controller password, the controller log may show only that shared identity. Correlation with a unique gateway session and application audit can help reconstruct actions, but simultaneous sessions and incomplete logging can make the mapping ambiguous. Prefer controlled workflows that retain individual accountability where supported, while documenting legacy limitations instead of claiming that an unsupported controller can perform modern identity functions.

Assess effective privilege through group membership, nested roles, local accounts, service permissions, API tokens and stored credentials. An account described as read-only in a procedure may inherit administration through another group or possess a private key for a more privileged service. Evaluate deny/allow precedence according to the actual platform; do not assume a generic rule order across identity systems. Separate the right to connect from the right to change process state, administer security, approve a change and erase evidence. Concentrating all of these in one identity weakens separation of duties and recovery confidence.

MFA is a control at a defined authentication point. Determine which paths enforce it, which factors are used, how enrollment and recovery work, and whether existing sessions or service tokens remain valid after account disablement. Phishing-resistant mechanisms can reduce particular credential-theft paths, but downstream shared secrets, unmanaged sessions and alternate local accounts still need analysis. A bypass or break-glass account may be operationally necessary during identity-provider failure; it must have deliberate custody, use conditions, monitoring, rotation and restoration to normal access.

Identity availability is an OT dependency. Central authentication failure may block new engineering sessions while existing control continues. A recovery action may require an identity service that is itself unavailable during the incident. Test the intended degraded mode in a representative environment: which local access remains, who can invoke it, what commands are allowed and how evidence is retained. Emergency access that is impossible to use under the failure scenario is not a reliable safeguard; emergency access that is always open and unmonitored creates a standing alternate path.

Service and device identities require lifecycle controls even when no human types a password. Track certificate validity, trust anchors, private-key protection, token scope and rotation. Expired certificates can interrupt telemetry or remote access; overly broad trust stores can accept unintended peers. Revocation behavior depends on the implementation and network availability. Offline devices may not consult online status services, so the assessment should verify the actual policy and compensating mechanisms rather than treating certificate presence as complete identity assurance.

Review joiner, mover and leaver events using evidence. Disablement in the corporate directory may not revoke a cached gateway session, a locally stored engineering password, a long-lived API token or a separate vendor account. Define the expected revocation latency and test the full chain under approved conditions. Preserve service continuity when rotating credentials that support polling or backups. Findings should identify the exact identity, effective capability, path, lifecycle gap and consequence, with an implementable treatment and a way to verify that it works.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — IDENTITY CHAIN (synthetic): Named vendor Alice authenticates to R using MFA; R issues a session valid for 8 hours. Disabling Alice in D1 blocks new logins but does not revoke existing R sessions. R's jump host J uses shared controller account eng_shared. J allows two concurrent vendor sessions. Controller C logs only eng_shared and command time. Group MonitorReaders inherits GatewayAdmins through a nested group; svc_metrics belongs to MonitorReaders. Emergency local account rescue_ot is sealed in a controlled cabinet, but the access procedure requires approval through an application hosted on D1. Device certificate for telemetry gateway T expires in 10 days; T does not support online certificate-status checking, and trust-store maintenance ownership is unassigned.
worked_examples.solution:
Disabling Alice at D1 does not satisfy immediate end-to-end revocation because an existing R session can remain valid for up to its remaining lifetime. The assessment should examine R's session revocation mechanism and define a bounded disablement workflow. Controller attribution is ambiguous if two vendor sessions can issue commands through eng_shared and no application-level session mapping is retained; a timestamp alone may not uniquely identify the human actor.

svc_metrics has effective GatewayAdmins membership through nesting despite its read-oriented group name. That privilege must be verified and evaluated against the service's actual needs. The emergency procedure contains a circular recovery dependency: D1 failure may make the approval application unavailable precisely when rescue_ot is needed. Establish an authorized alternate approval and evidence route, not an uncontrolled standing bypass. T's approaching expiry is an availability concern, while absent online status support and unassigned trust-store ownership require a deliberate device-trust lifecycle. Do not claim that lack of online checking automatically invalidates every certificate; assess the supported trust and revocation design.

guided_practice.prompt: A vendor contract ends at noon while its API token remains valid until midnight. Propose an evidence-based revocation acceptance test.
guided_practice.hint: Test both new authentication and already issued authority.
guided_practice.solution: In an authorized representative environment, disable the vendor identity at the defined time, revoke active sessions and tokens through supported mechanisms, then verify new login denial and denial of an attempted privileged API operation using the previously issued token. Confirm required service accounts remain functional and audit records preserve who revoked access and when. State the maximum permitted propagation delay and verify it.

independent_task.brief: Build a privilege and revocation table for the supplied identities, including emergency operation during D1 loss.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Effective nested privileges and existing-session lifetime are evaluated.
Human attribution limitations through the shared account are explicit.
Emergency access remains authorized and usable when the primary identity service is unavailable.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.
