lessons.title: Remote access, wireless bridges and supplier trust paths
lessons.body:
Remote access is an operational workflow spanning people, endpoints, identity services, communication paths, intermediaries and target functions. A VPN encrypts a transport segment; it does not by itself decide whether a vendor should change a controller setpoint, whether the source laptop is trustworthy, or whether the session is approved for the current operating mode. Trace where encryption terminates, where identity is verified, where authorization is enforced and where process commands become possible.

A mediated maintenance design commonly uses an externally reachable gateway, a controlled intermediary in a defined boundary zone and narrowly permitted access to target engineering services. Assessment should verify actual routing and application behavior rather than infer this structure from product names. A gateway that forwards a broad network route to the vendor laptop creates different exposure from a broker that exposes only a specific application session. Split tunneling, local network access and endpoint compromise can connect the remote session to other networks or identities outside the owner's control.

Assess supplier endpoints and support practices within the contractual and technical evidence available. Relevant questions include device management, patch and malware protection, privileged access, credential storage, remote-control software, subcontractor access, session approval and incident notification. A supplier questionnaire is useful evidence but does not replace technical enforcement at the owner's boundary. Use time-bounded access, explicit target/function authorization and owner-controlled revocation where supported. Record who can enable the path and how an emergency session differs from routine maintenance.

Wireless introduces a physical propagation boundary that rarely matches a cabinet or fence. An access point's signal may extend beyond the intended work area; association security and authenticated authorization must therefore carry the trust decision. Hidden network names and MAC allowlists offer little resistance to an actor who can observe or imitate identifiers. Enterprise authentication can bind device or user identity to network policy, but certificate validation, credential enrollment and role assignment still need examination. Guest and maintenance SSIDs sharing a radio do not automatically share a trust zone, and separate SSIDs do not automatically prove isolation.

A wireless or cellular bridge may bypass a wired firewall. Verify whether it routes, bridges, performs address translation or proxies an application, and identify the effective source addresses seen by the target. NAT can conceal multiple upstream principals behind one address, weakening IP-based attribution. A protocol gateway translating serial traffic may expose only one IP endpoint while granting access to many downstream stations. Assess the final command reach and authorization, not merely the visible IP count.

Remote sessions need monitoring with defined response. Record login, approval, target, privilege elevation, relevant command or application activity and termination where the platforms support it. A recording that no one can review until after an incident is still potentially valuable evidence, but it is not rapid detection. Define how a suspicious session is terminated without creating an unsafe partial process change. Session timeout, idle timeout and account expiry are different controls; a busy unauthorized session may never hit an idle timeout.

Evaluate failure and recovery behavior. If the access gateway fails, local control should behave according to the approved architecture, and emergency support should have a controlled alternative if required. A fail-open bypass may preserve connectivity while violating the very boundary the gateway enforces. A fail-closed path may be appropriate for remote maintenance but can still impair urgent recovery if no authorized fallback exists. The assessment should state the intended failure mode for each function, validate it in a representative environment and include the path in lifecycle change and revocation reviews.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — REMOTE PATH FACTS (synthetic): Vendor VPN terminates on firewall F in the enterprise zone. Its route permits 10.120.0.0/24. F allows TCP/3389 only to jump host J, but J can reach all TCP ports on OT subnet 10.130.0.0/24. An unmanaged maintenance AP bridges a service SSID directly into 10.130.0.0/24; it uses a shared WPA2 passphrase and a hidden SSID. A cellular gateway N translates all remote vendor sources to 10.130.0.9 and can reach serial gateway G. Session logs at G record only source 10.130.0.9. J's idle timeout is 15 minutes; maximum session duration is unset. A vendor account can establish an active session outside any approved maintenance window. F's failure removes the VPN path but leaves the AP and N paths available.
worked_examples.solution:
The VPN's encryption terminates in the enterprise zone, and the supplied F rule restricts the first application hop to J. J's broad OT access remains a separate authorization boundary: an authenticated session on J can potentially reach many unnecessary target services unless host, application and downstream controls narrow it. The AP and cellular gateway create additional paths that do not depend on F, so F cannot be credited as comprehensive remote-access enforcement.

A hidden SSID does not make the AP an authenticated isolated conduit. The shared passphrase weakens individual revocation and attribution, while bridging places associated clients into the OT network's Layer 2 context. N's translation means G's source-IP log cannot distinguish remote individuals; upstream identity/session evidence must be correlated or the architecture changed. Fifteen-minute idle timeout does not bound a continuously active session, and it does not enforce a maintenance window. The assessment should define required functions and owner-approved access conditions, then test each actual path's admission, reach, logging and termination behavior.

guided_practice.prompt: A supplier says its VPN is secure because it uses strong encryption. Write three additional technical questions that determine the risk of its OT access.
guided_practice.hint: Encryption covers a transport property; assess endpoint authority and the final command path.
guided_practice.solution: Which identities and managed endpoints can establish the tunnel and how are existing sessions revoked? Which exact target functions become reachable after termination, including alternate AP/cellular paths? What owner approval, command/session evidence and safe termination mechanism apply during the intended maintenance window?

independent_task.brief: Create a conduit register for F–J, the maintenance AP and N–G, with authentication, authorization, visibility, owner and failure behavior.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Every remote path is represented through its final target capability.
Encryption is separated from process authorization and individual attribution.
Idle timeout, maximum duration and maintenance-window enforcement are distinguished.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Physical access, removable media and configuration supply chains
lessons.body:
A network boundary does not contain every cyber entry path. Portable engineering laptops, removable storage, replacement controller modules, vendor firmware, service serial cables and configuration files can introduce code or authority without a routed connection from an external network. Begin by listing how software, logic, credentials and maintenance tools enter each zone. Follow the artifact from its origin through receipt, verification, storage, transfer, installation and recovery use.

Physical access can enable different capabilities at different devices. Opening a cabinet may expose a console port, removable storage slot, reset button or network connection, but it does not automatically bypass every authentication or firmware-signature check. Conversely, a locked cabinet may share keys widely or remain open during maintenance. Assess access authorization, key or badge custody, visitor escort, records, tamper evidence and the practical response to an observed violation. Security measures around energized equipment must be coordinated with qualified personnel and applicable site safety arrangements; this course does not authorize opening live cabinets.

Removable-media controls need a complete workflow. An intake station can scan files, verify approved origin and signatures, and record custody before transfer. Malware scanning does not prove that a file is the correct engineering project for the target asset or that every malicious modification will be detected. Digital signatures can establish a relationship to a signing key and protect integrity of signed content when validation is correct; they do not establish that the signer is authorized for this site or that the signed firmware is compatible and free of vulnerabilities. Match the artifact to the approved product, version, change and asset.

A media process can fail through recontamination. A USB device scanned before visiting an unmanaged laptop may carry different content when later inserted into OT. Record the sequence and use controlled media or transfer mechanisms suited to the environment. Treat bidirectional portable devices as conduits between trust domains, even if they are not continuously connected. Where operationally suitable, use write-protected or single-purpose transfer methods and verify the received artifact's integrity at the destination. A one-way workflow still needs correct origin, content and installation authorization.

Supply-chain assessment includes both supplier practices and local verification. Obtain supported firmware through an authenticated approved channel, verify the supplier's published authenticity/integrity mechanism using an independently trusted reference, and retain the package identifier and validation evidence. A checksum downloaded from the same compromised location as a file can be replaced along with the file, so it is weaker than a signature anchored in a separately maintained trusted key. An internal checksum remains useful for detecting changes after receipt, provided its provenance is clear.

Replacement and recovery create special trust transitions. A spare can arrive with an old firmware baseline, default accounts or an unknown configuration even when its model matches the failed asset. Commission it through the approved baseline process before treating it as equivalent. Recovered project files may contain malicious changes if the backup predates discovery but follows the initial compromise. Select a known-good recovery point using evidence, validate process configuration and maintain provenance rather than assuming every backup is trustworthy.

Document chain of custody proportionately. For a critical project download, retain who obtained the file, where it came from, the signature or digest result, approval, target identity, tool version, transfer path, installation time and post-change verification. The assessment should identify where the chain can be substituted, modified or misapplied. Treatments can include restricted physical access, trusted artifact repositories, controlled portable devices, application allowlisting, independent change review and verified recovery copies. Each control should be evaluated against the actual path rather than credited simply because a policy exists.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — MAINTENANCE ARTIFACT CASE (synthetic): Vendor sends signed firmware package FW-9 for controller hardware revision B. Site controller C is revision A; compatibility is unverified. The package and its SHA-256 text file arrive from the same download portal. The site trusts signing key K from an approved offline key register; signature validation has not yet been performed. USB U is scanned at intake, then connected to an unmanaged contractor laptop, then taken to the OT engineering station. Cabinet keys are shared among twelve contractors with no issue log. A replacement controller of the correct model arrives with default credentials. Backup P was created after an unexplained project change but before the incident was recognized.
worked_examples.solution:
The package cannot be approved for C merely because it is signed: authenticity validation is not yet performed, and hardware compatibility remains unresolved. Validate the signature against the independently trusted K according to the supported method, then verify the package's authorized applicability to revision A. The checksum can detect accidental or later changes, but its same-portal origin alone does not provide independent authenticity if that portal is compromised.

U's intake scan no longer describes its final state after connection to the unmanaged laptop. The transfer chain needs revalidation or a controlled replacement workflow before OT use. Shared cabinet keys without issue records weaken accountability for physical entry. The replacement controller needs baseline commissioning and credential treatment despite matching the model. Backup P is not automatically a known-good recovery source because the suspicious change preceded it; compare version history, approved changes and process configuration evidence to select and validate a suitable recovery point.

guided_practice.prompt: Design a controlled transfer record for a controller project arriving from an integrator. Include five checks beyond antivirus scanning.
guided_practice.hint: Track both artifact trust and correct application to the target process.
guided_practice.solution: Verify approved sender/channel and custody; validate the supported signature or independent integrity reference; match project and tool version to the exact target asset/hardware; obtain change approval and independent configuration review; preserve a verified rollback baseline; then confirm post-download configuration and intended process behavior in the authorized environment.

independent_task.brief: Draw the artifact path from vendor to controller and mark substitution, recontamination, wrong-target and untrusted-recovery opportunities.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Signature authenticity, compatibility and owner authorization are separate decisions.
The USB sequence is analyzed at the point of OT entry.
Replacement and backup trust are established through evidence, not names or dates alone.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Initial risk screening and assessment prioritization
lessons.body:
Initial risk screening identifies where a more detailed assessment is needed and establishes a common consequence language. It should be quick enough to cover the system but specific enough to distinguish functions. Begin with the process and service inventory, existing hazard information, operating modes, dependencies and broadly plausible cyber events. The screen may assume loss or misuse of a function before detailed safeguards are analyzed, but that assumption must be explicit. Otherwise one team may rate an uncontrolled consequence while another silently credits several protections, making their scores incomparable.

Define the consequence scale with observable thresholds. For availability, categories might distinguish loss of one monitoring point, temporary loss of a redundant train, interruption of a critical service beyond its recovery objective, and a site-wide interruption. Safety and environmental dimensions need their own owner-approved criteria and qualified interpretation. Financial bands may be useful but should not erase nonfinancial obligations or imply that personnel harm can be traded away by a simple arithmetic offset. Specify how multiple dimensions produce the reported category, such as taking the highest applicable severity under the organization's approved method.

Define the likelihood scale and the meaning of a rating. A qualitative category such as low, medium or high is not a measured annual probability unless the method supplies calibrated definitions and evidence. An initial screen may use exposure and plausible initiating events to prioritize work, with explicit low confidence. Avoid using the number of known vulnerabilities as a direct likelihood measure: one exposed process-changing credential can matter more than many low-impact software findings. Do not let an unknown inventory produce an artificially low score simply because few weaknesses have been discovered.

A matrix is a decision aid, not a physical law. If the organization maps likelihood categories 1–3 and consequence categories 1–4 to priority bands, use that mapping consistently and retain the underlying categories. Multiplying ordinal labels can produce ties between scenarios with very different meanings. A high-consequence/low-likelihood scenario may deserve a mandatory review even when its numerical product equals a moderate scenario. State any override rule and who owns it. Do not compare scores from different scales as if they were common units.

Initial zone proposals help bound the next analysis. Group assets by function, criticality and provisional security requirements, then identify important communications between groups. This is a hypothesis for detailed review, not a final security architecture. Assets sharing an IP subnet may have different consequences, and assets in separate subnets may share management or recovery dependencies. The initial screen should flag common-cause paths, external access, unsupported components and high-consequence functions for deeper assessment.

Document uncertainty as an output. A scenario with severe credible consequences and missing control evidence may be a high assessment priority even if its final residual risk cannot yet be estimated. Separate 'risk appears high based on current evidence' from 'assessment priority is high because evidence is insufficient'. This distinction prevents pressure to invent ratings and helps assign evidence-collection work. Track the assumptions that could move the category, the owners who can resolve them and the decision that depends on the result.

The screening report should lead to a planned detailed assessment: selected functions and scenarios, required participants, evidence needs, provisional zone/conduit questions and the reasons for prioritization. Reconcile the screen with current operating constraints and near-term changes. A low screening priority is not permanent acceptance, particularly when architecture, exposure or process consequences change. The next stages refine threat events, vulnerabilities, safeguards, likelihood and residual consequences using the documented criteria.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — INITIAL SCREEN METHOD (synthetic local method, not an ISA-prescribed matrix): Likelihood categories L1 limited opportunity, L2 credible opportunity, L3 frequent opportunity. Consequence C1 minor local effect, C2 loss of redundancy within recovery objective, C3 critical service interruption beyond objective, C4 severe safety/environmental consequence requiring qualified review. Numerical product is used only for queue ordering: 1–3 routine, 4–6 priority, 8–12 urgent. Mandatory overrides: every C4 and every unknown safeguard for a credible C3/C4 scenario requires detailed assessment. Scenario A: cooling remote-write misuse, L2/C3, safeguard evidence unknown. B: isolated spare historian loss, L3/C1. C: rare protective-function interference, L1/C4. D: one redundant telemetry feed loss, L2/C2. No category is a measured annual probability.
worked_examples.solution:
A has a numerical product of 6, placing it in the priority queue, and independently requires detailed assessment because safeguard evidence is unknown for a credible C3 scenario. B scores 3 and is routine under this local queue method, despite its more frequent opportunity, because the supplied consequence is minor and the spare is isolated. C scores 4 but requires mandatory qualified detailed review because C4 overrides the product band. D scores 4 and is priority without the supplied mandatory override.

The equal product for C and D does not make them equivalent risks: their consequence dimensions and review obligations differ. None of L1, L2 or L3 can be read as an annual probability without additional calibration. The screen should preserve the L/C categories, override rationale and uncertainty, then schedule deeper work on the relevant functions. It should not claim that C's severe outcome is accepted simply because the numerical product is modest, or that A's unknown safeguards are absent or effective without evidence.

guided_practice.prompt: A new cellular path reaches the isolated spare in B and the spare is repurposed as the only operational historian. Explain what must be rescreened.
guided_practice.hint: Both exposure and consequence assumptions changed.
guided_practice.solution: Revisit the opportunity category because external reachability changed; revisit the consequence because the asset is no longer an isolated spare and now supports a unique operational/evidence function; identify new dependencies and controls; update the provisional zone/conduit model and assessment priority. Do not retain L3/C1 merely because the asset name is unchanged.

independent_task.brief: Apply the supplied screening method to four new clearly stated synthetic functions and justify categories, overrides and evidence priorities.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Underlying likelihood and consequence categories remain visible beside the queue product.
C4 and unknown-safeguard override rules are applied correctly.
The output is an assessment plan rather than an unsupported final acceptance.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Detailed likelihood, conditional events and uncertainty
lessons.body:
Detailed likelihood analysis asks how plausible the defined scenario is under the assessed conditions and time horizon. Separate the occurrence of a threat event from the probability that it produces an adverse impact. A vendor credential may be stolen without granting a usable engineering session; a usable session may not reach the required function; a malicious command may be blocked or its consequence limited. Combining all of these into one intuitive high/medium/low label can hide the control assumptions that matter most.

Use an event tree or conditional chain where it clarifies reasoning. Let A be a credential theft during the next year, B be successful session establishment given A, and C be a harmful command accepted given A and B. The joint probability is P(A) × P(B given A) × P(C given A and B). This multiplication follows the chain rule when the conditional quantities are correctly defined; it does not require pretending that the events are independent. In practice, credible numerical estimates may be unavailable. An ordinal or bounded assessment with explicit uncertainty is preferable to unsupported decimals.

Differentiate probability and frequency. A probability of at least one relevant event within a year is not the same as an expected number of attempts per year. A probability must lie between zero and one, while expected counts may exceed one. Do not multiply a count by another count and call the result a probability. If repeated attempts share the same credentials or control weakness, their outcomes may be strongly dependent. A simple independent-trials model should not be used without defending that assumption and the stability of conditions over the interval.

Control dependence is a central OT issue. Two gateways managed through the same privileged account may fail together under account compromise. MFA, account approval and logging may all depend on one identity service. Two process protections can share a sensor or power supply. Multiplying nominal failure probabilities as if each were independent can substantially understate the joint scenario. Identify common causes and model them explicitly or use a conservative bounded estimate until evidence supports a more detailed model.

Use evidence appropriate to the quantity. Historical incident counts can inform a baseline, but underreporting, changing exposure and small samples limit inference. A penetration test demonstrates a capability under test conditions, not an annual attack frequency. A vendor's control effectiveness claim may apply to a different configuration or threat class. Expert judgment can be valuable when its basis, dissent and confidence are recorded. Avoid averaging incompatible opinions before clarifying that the experts are estimating the same event, horizon and operating state.

Express uncertainty using ranges, alternative scenarios or sensitivity analysis. If successful session establishment is estimated between 0.1 and 0.4 conditional on credential theft, show how that range changes the overall result under the other stated assumptions. This identifies which evidence would most improve the decision. Do not label an interval a statistical confidence interval unless it was derived by an appropriate statistical method. An elicited plausible range is a different kind of statement.

Likelihood also changes over time. A new exploit, exposed maintenance tunnel, expired control exception or altered supplier workflow can invalidate a previous estimate. Record the observation date, configuration baseline and update triggers. The final scenario record should preserve the initiating event, conditional transitions, supporting evidence, dependence assumptions, uncertainty and the effect of existing controls. The purpose is a defensible engineering decision, not a superficially precise number that obscures unknowns.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — ILLUSTRATIVE EVENT MODEL — numbers are supplied teaching assumptions, not measured facility probabilities. Horizon: next 12 months. A=at least one theft of a relevant vendor credential, P(A)=0.20. B=usable remote session given A, P(B|A)=0.30. C=harmful command accepted given A and B, P(C|A,B)=0.40. D=process protection fails to prevent the defined consequence given A,B,C, P(D|A,B,C)=0.50. Estimated B range is 0.10–0.40. Two nominally redundant gateways share one privileged management account. A separate record reports 2.4 phishing attempts per vendor-year; it is an expected attempt count, not P(A). A lab exercise demonstrated C once under an intentionally permissive configuration.
worked_examples.solution:
Under the supplied conditional model, the joint probability of A, B, C and D is 0.20 × 0.30 × 0.40 × 0.50 = 0.012, or 1.2% over the stated 12-month horizon. This is the output of an illustrative model, not a measured site prediction. Replacing B with its supplied lower and upper bounds yields 0.004 to 0.016, or 0.4% to 1.6%, while holding the other assumptions fixed. That is a sensitivity range, not a statistically derived confidence interval.

The 2.4 expected attempts cannot be substituted directly for P(A), because it is a count and can exceed one. It also concerns attempts rather than successful credential theft. The shared gateway administrator is a common-cause condition that can defeat assumptions of independent gateway failure. The lab demonstration supports capability in its permissive configuration but does not estimate the annual frequency or production conditional probability without further evidence. The assessment should identify these limits and prioritize evidence about session establishment, actual configuration and common administrative dependencies.

guided_practice.prompt: A reviewer multiplies two gateway compromise probabilities of 0.1 to claim joint compromise probability 0.01, although both use the same stolen administrator credential. Explain the flaw and an improved model.
guided_practice.hint: Identify the common event that can affect both gateways at once.
guided_practice.solution: The product assumes an independence relationship that shared administrator compromise contradicts. Model credential compromise as a common initiating event and evaluate each gateway takeover conditional on that event, including any distinct controls. If conditional evidence is missing, report a bounded or qualitative common-cause scenario rather than the unsupported 0.01 claim.

independent_task.brief: Create a likelihood worksheet separating initiating event, conditional transitions, units, horizon, evidence and dependence assumptions.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The supplied chain gives 1.2% with its assumptions clearly labeled.
The B sensitivity range is distinguished from a statistical confidence interval.
Attempt frequency and event probability are not mixed.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Consequence propagation, service recovery and common dependencies
lessons.body:
Consequence analysis should explain how a cyber-induced change propagates through the facility's functions. Start with the affected capability: a meter stops reporting, a gateway returns stale values, a controller loses logic, an engineering station cannot authenticate, or a historian becomes unavailable. Trace what continues locally, what operators can no longer see or command, which dependent systems rely on the information and how long degraded operation is acceptable. Do not equate loss of supervisory visibility with automatic loss of every local protective function, but do not dismiss visibility loss when operators need it to recognize a developing condition.

Distinguish availability, integrity and timing. A live-looking value with an old timestamp can be more misleading than an explicit communication-failed indicator. A delayed command may be unsafe if the process has moved into another state by the time it executes. Incorrect event order can mislead incident diagnosis even when the devices continued operating. State the quality and freshness information required by each consumer and evaluate how it behaves when those properties are missing or wrong.

Map dependencies as required functions rather than only infrastructure boxes. An EPMS alarm may require meter acquisition, gateway polling, message transport, application processing, time correlation, display and operator response. A recovery workflow may require backup access, decryption keys, compatible software, licensing, identity services and trained staff. Identify which stages can run concurrently and which must wait. A nominal backup restoration time does not include prerequisites unless the procedure explicitly measures them.

Define recovery objectives carefully. A recovery time objective is the target time to restore the specified service after an agreed event reference; it is not automatically the maximum tolerable process interruption or a measured restoration duration. A recovery point objective bounds acceptable data loss in time for the specified data set. A four-hour RPO does not mean the system may remain offline for four hours. Some controller configurations require zero unapproved logic loss even if a historian can tolerate a bounded telemetry gap. Different functions need different objectives and evidence.

Calculate recovery timelines using the critical path. If replacement hardware preparation and backup retrieval occur in parallel, the next dependent stage starts after the slower branch completes. Include detection, decision, access and validation, not just file copying. Record whether durations are measured, vendor estimates or exercise assumptions. A fast restoration of an untrusted image may recreate the compromise; a validated clean recovery can require additional time. Evaluate the consequence of degraded operation during that period and the conditions under which operations must stop or shift to a fallback.

Common dependencies can defeat redundancy and recovery together. Two applications on separate hosts may share storage, a directory, a license server or a privileged backup account. A ransomware scenario can make the availability of storage and the integrity of backups correlated. A generator-backed server may still depend on an unprotected network switch. The assessment should identify the minimum combinations of lost functions that produce the adverse outcome and verify the claimed independence of alternatives.

Report consequences with operational meaning and uncertainty. Describe affected halls, trains, monitoring points or services; duration and operating mode; data loss or integrity uncertainty; possible safety/environmental implications for qualified review; and downstream recovery obligations. Separate maximum credible consequence under stated conditions from expected or typical loss. Use scenario alternatives where facts are uncertain. The result should support treatment decisions and measurable recovery requirements rather than a generic statement that downtime is expensive.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — RECOVERY CASE (synthetic): G aggregates 40 electrical meters. G failure removes remote telemetry and alarms, but local meter displays and independent protective relays continue. The EPMS service RTO is 90 minutes from detection; historian RPO is 15 minutes. Recovery sequence after detection: decision/authorization 10 min; then spare preparation 25 min and backup retrieval 40 min in parallel; firmware/configuration load 20 min after both; functional validation 15 min. Latest historian backup is 35 minutes old at the failure point. Both primary and standby EPMS VMs use datastore DS and the same backup administrator. HMI last-value display remains green indefinitely when telemetry stops unless a separate freshness rule is enabled; that rule is currently disabled.
worked_examples.solution:
The recovery critical path is 10 + max(25,40) + 20 + 15 = 85 minutes from detection, leaving five minutes against the 90-minute RTO under the supplied exercise durations. Adding the two parallel branches would incorrectly produce 110 minutes; omitting validation would incorrectly imply service restoration at 70 minutes. The five-minute margin is small and does not include unmodeled delays, so representative exercise evidence is needed before relying on it.

The 35-minute-old historian backup exceeds the 15-minute RPO by 20 minutes if no other validated data source can close the gap. This is a data-loss issue separate from the 85-minute restoration timeline. G loss removes remote visibility and alarms but does not, on the supplied facts, disable local displays or independent relays. The indefinitely green last value creates an integrity/freshness concern because operators may interpret stale telemetry as current. Shared DS and backup administration weaken both redundancy and recovery independence and should be modeled as common-cause scenarios rather than treated as two independent VM services.

guided_practice.prompt: Backup retrieval is improved to 15 minutes while spare preparation remains 25 minutes. Calculate the new recovery time and identify the new critical branch.
guided_practice.hint: The next stage still waits for both parallel branches.
guided_practice.solution: The timeline becomes 10 + max(25,15) + 20 + 15 = 70 minutes. Spare preparation is now the longer parallel branch. Further speeding retrieval below 15 minutes will not shorten the total for this model unless it changes another dependency; improve the critical branch or another sequential stage to reduce the total.

independent_task.brief: Create a service consequence and recovery timeline for loss of G, including freshness, local fallback and common-cause limitations.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: RTO and RPO are applied to the correct service/data quantities.
Parallel work uses the critical path and includes validation.
Local protection, supervisory visibility and stale-data integrity are distinguished.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Crediting safeguards through technical evidence
lessons.body:
A safeguard should receive credit only for the scenario conditions it actually changes. A firewall can restrict selected network paths, an application role can restrict commands, an intrusion detector can reveal suspicious activity, a protective function can limit physical consequences, and a backup can support recovery. These functions are complementary but not interchangeable. Write the claimed mechanism before evaluating the evidence: which transition does the control block, which event does it detect, which consequence does it reduce, or which service does it restore?

For preventive network controls, inspect the effective policy and actual traffic path. A first-match rule base can contain a specific deny that never applies because an earlier broad permit matches first. A port-level permit for an industrial protocol may allow both read and write operations unless the control performs and enforces suitable application-level inspection. A rule's presence does not prove packets traverse it; alternate routes, dual-homed hosts and local maintenance access may bypass the enforcement point. Review source and destination semantics, direction, state handling, address translation and rule order for the actual platform.

For detection, distinguish visibility, recognition and response. A sensor must receive the relevant traffic or events, parse the protocol or otherwise detect the behavior, generate an actionable alert, and reach a responder who can act within the process time available. High packet-volume coverage can coexist with complete blindness to a low-volume critical command path. Encrypted or proprietary protocols may limit content inspection. A detection percentage quoted without a defined test set, false-positive burden, operating state and response process is not a reliable site effectiveness estimate.

For procedural safeguards, examine execution conditions. A two-person review requires qualified independent reviewers, access to the correct baseline and enough time to detect relevant errors. A change ticket approved after the work does not prevent the initial change. A maintenance-window policy needs a technical or operational mechanism that actually controls access when the window is closed. A training record can support competence, but it does not prove that an individual followed the procedure during a particular session.

For recovery controls, verify both artifact availability and service restoration. Backups need correct content, suitable recovery points, protected access, compatible tools and tested procedures. Redundant equipment needs failure independence and a functioning transfer or failover mechanism. A successful test performed with production identity services available may not establish recovery after those services fail. Credit the control for the conditions represented by the test and record untested dependencies.

Use an evidence hierarchy without making it absolute. Current implemented configuration, observed behavior and representative tests often provide stronger support than a policy statement, but each has limits. A test can cover only the exercised conditions; a configuration can be bypassed by another path; a log may be incomplete or untrustworthy. Combine evidence and record its freshness. Supplier certification can support component capability under its defined scope but does not prove correct integration or operational maintenance at this site.

Avoid double counting. A firewall rule and the same rule's appearance in a compliance dashboard are one mechanism with two evidence views, not two independent barriers. Two alarms sourced from one compromised measurement do not provide independent detection. If multiple safeguards share power, identity, management or data, identify the common cause. A control ledger should state the scenario transition, mechanism, scope, evidence, limitations, owner, validation result and reassessment trigger. This makes residual-risk reasoning explicit and allows the design team to see exactly which requirements are still unmet.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — SYNTHETIC CONTROL EVIDENCE: Firewall uses first-match rules: R1 allow J→C any TCP; R2 deny J→C TCP/502; R3 allow H→C TCP/502; R4 deny all remaining. J is the engineering jump host; H is a historian intended only to read. Firewall performs no Modbus function inspection. A separate local maintenance port on C bypasses this firewall. IDS receives 95% of total site packet volume but none of the maintenance-port traffic; it cannot parse the proprietary engineering protocol. Alert triage occurs next business day. The process response window for the assessed harmful change is 8 minutes. Backup restoration was tested with D1 available; the recovery procedure requires D1 and has no tested alternate identity path.
worked_examples.solution:
R2 does not deny J's Modbus traffic because R1 already permits any TCP from J to C. Rule ordering makes the specific deny ineffective for that matched path. R3 permits TCP/502 from H but cannot enforce read-only Modbus semantics without application-aware enforcement or an appropriate endpoint restriction. The local maintenance port is outside this firewall's coverage entirely.

The IDS's 95% packet-volume figure is not sufficient evidence for the assessed command scenario: its blind path and unsupported protocol may be precisely where the harmful action occurs. Next-business-day triage cannot satisfy an eight-minute process-response need. The IDS may still support later investigation for observed traffic, but it should not be credited as timely prevention. The backup test demonstrates restoration only with D1 available; an incident affecting D1 can invalidate that recovery assumption. The control ledger should record these bounded credits and gaps rather than counting firewall, IDS and backup as three fully effective independent safeguards.

guided_practice.prompt: An auditor sees R2 and concludes engineering writes are blocked. Specify an analytical check and a representative validation that challenge that conclusion.
guided_practice.hint: Evaluate the first matching rule and the protocol-operation scope.
guided_practice.solution: Trace a J-to-C TCP/502 flow through ordered rules: R1 matches first, so R2 is not reached. In an isolated authorized policy model or supported representative firewall, verify the effective match and the allowed connection; use synthetic command semantics or a safe read-only test rather than issuing live process writes. Separately evaluate whether any control distinguishes Modbus read and write functions.

independent_task.brief: Complete a control ledger for the firewall, IDS and backup with one supported credit and at least one limitation for each.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Rule order and application-versus-port authorization are interpreted correctly.
Detection credit includes coverage, interpretation and response latency.
Common dependencies and alternate paths prevent double counting.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

cards.back: A specific scenario transition, detectable event, consequence or recovery function, with evidence of actual coverage and behavior.

lessons.title: Risk estimation, residual risk and decision confidence
lessons.body:
Risk estimation combines the likelihood of the defined scenario with the magnitude and character of its consequences. The method may be qualitative, semi-quantitative or quantitative, but it must preserve what the inputs mean. An ordinal matrix can support consistent categories; an expected-loss model can support financial comparison when probabilities and losses are defensible. Neither method eliminates safety, environmental, contractual or regulatory obligations, and neither grants the assessor authority to accept the result.

Separate inherent or initial risk from residual risk by stating the control basis. One organization may use inherent to mean no credited safeguards, while another includes basic physical features of the plant. Define the term before using it. Residual risk is the scenario risk remaining after the controls actually included in the assessment, not the risk after every proposed measure has been assumed successful. Label forecast residual risk for a planned design separately from validated residual risk for implemented controls. A treatment schedule does not reduce current exposure by itself.

For a numerical expected-loss example, multiply the probability of each mutually exclusive outcome by its corresponding loss and sum the products. If outcomes overlap, simple addition may double count the same loss or event. Keep the horizon consistent and distinguish one-time capital cost from annual operating cost and annual expected loss. An expected value is a long-run model average, not a prediction that the organization will lose exactly that amount next year. Rare severe events can produce a modest average while remaining unacceptable under a consequence-based rule.

Use ranges and sensitivity analysis to show decision robustness. If the estimated reduction depends heavily on an unverified detection probability, vary that input across a plausible range. If every plausible result exceeds the owner's threshold, the decision is less sensitive to precise calibration. If the range crosses the threshold, additional evidence or a precautionary treatment may be warranted. Do not selectively choose the favorable end of a range to manufacture acceptance. Record who supplied the estimates and what would change them.

Avoid transferring uncertainty into hidden arithmetic. A matrix label based on unknown safeguard effectiveness should retain that uncertainty rather than presenting a crisp low residual category. A monetary estimate should state which losses are included and excluded, such as equipment damage, lost service, contractual penalties, recovery labor and wider safety or environmental consequences. Some dimensions may be assessed separately because monetization would be inappropriate or unsupported. The report should not imply that an omitted dimension has zero value.

Risk acceptance is a governance decision informed by engineering evidence. Identify the accountable owner, applicable criteria, required escalations, conditions, expiry and monitoring triggers. A decision may accept a temporary exception with compensating controls and a replacement deadline. That is different from a permanent declaration of adequacy. Acceptance cannot waive obligations beyond the owner's authority, and a signed form does not make an ineffective control technically effective. The assessor should state the evidence-based conclusion candidly, including disagreement or unresolved limitations.

Maintain traceability from each final rating back to the scenario, threat conditions, vulnerabilities, consequences, controls and evidence. Record how proposed treatment changes the model and what test would justify moving from forecast to implemented residual risk. This makes the result useful for design requirements and later reassessment. The aim is not a single attractive number but a decision whose assumptions and consequences remain visible to the people responsible for the system.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — ILLUSTRATIVE FINANCIAL MODEL (synthetic, annual horizon; not calibrated site loss data): Mutually exclusive outcomes for one scenario are minor interruption with probability 0.10 and loss USD 20,000; major interruption with probability 0.02 and loss USD 500,000; no modeled interruption otherwise. Current expected loss includes service and recovery costs only. Proposed control X forecasts reducing major probability to 0.005 while minor probability stays 0.10; implementation is not complete. X costs USD 30,000 once plus USD 4,000 per year to operate. Owner's annual expected-loss threshold is USD 6,000, but any credible severe safety consequence requires a separate qualified review regardless of money. Uncertainty range for X's major probability is 0.003–0.015. The assessor may recommend; the facility director accepts eligible residual risk.
worked_examples.solution:
Current expected annual loss is 0.10 × USD 20,000 + 0.02 × USD 500,000 = USD 2,000 + USD 10,000 = USD 12,000. The forecast after X at the central assumption is USD 2,000 + 0.005 × USD 500,000 = USD 4,500. The estimated annual reduction is USD 7,500 before X's USD 4,000 annual operating cost, leaving USD 3,500 annual net benefit in this limited model. A simple undiscounted payback on the USD 30,000 capital cost would be about 8.57 years if all assumptions stayed fixed; this is not a full investment appraisal.

The uncertainty range gives forecast expected loss from USD 3,500 to USD 9,500, which crosses the USD 6,000 threshold. The central estimate alone therefore does not establish robust acceptance. X is not implemented, so current risk remains based on existing controls. The monetary model excludes safety/environmental valuation, and the explicit severe-safety review rule still applies. The facility director needs the uncertainty, validation plan and any separate consequence review before an acceptance decision within that role's authority.

guided_practice.prompt: A report calls the forecast USD 4,500 residual loss implemented residual risk even though X is awaiting commissioning. Rewrite the conclusion and state the evidence needed to change its status.
guided_practice.hint: Distinguish design expectation from observed implemented control behavior.
guided_practice.solution: Current modeled expected loss remains USD 12,000 under the existing baseline. X forecasts USD 4,500 at the central assumptions, with a USD 3,500–USD 9,500 range and separate safety review conditions. After installation, verify X against the scenario-specific acceptance criteria, confirm operational compatibility and sustained control ownership, then update the residual estimate using the implemented evidence and obtain the appropriate acceptance decision.

independent_task.brief: Create a risk decision memo showing current, forecast and uncertainty results without treating expected value as a guaranteed annual loss.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The current and forecast expected losses are calculated correctly.
Annual operating cost and one-time capital cost remain distinct.
Threshold crossing, excluded consequence dimensions and acceptance authority are explicit.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

cards.front: What is expected loss?

lessons.title: Treatment selection, operational trade-offs and temporary exceptions
lessons.body:
Risk treatment changes the scenario or the decision about operating with it. Common strategies include avoiding the activity, reducing likelihood or consequence, sharing some consequences through contractual or financial arrangements, and explicitly retaining eligible residual risk. These are not interchangeable technical outcomes. Insurance may address selected financial losses while leaving a cooling failure's physical consequence unchanged. A supplier contract may allocate duties but does not itself enforce a firewall rule or restore a controller.

Start with the scenario's causal chain and the requirement that is not satisfied. A weak remote path might be treated by removing remote access, mediating it through a controlled gateway, restricting target functions, improving endpoint authorization, reducing process consequence through an independent safeguard, or improving recovery. Each option acts at a different point and creates different operational effects. Compare options against the same defined scenario and baseline so that a broad expensive control is not credited for benefits unrelated to the decision while a narrow effective control is dismissed because it lacks a fashionable label.

Identify constraints before scoring alternatives. These include process availability, supported firmware and application combinations, vendor warranty/support conditions, commissioning windows, physical space and power, staff capability, latency and protocol requirements, safety arrangements and recovery resources. A control that blocks all engineering traffic may prevent the attack path but also prevent required emergency restoration. This is not a reason to abandon security; it is a design requirement for a controlled authorized recovery workflow. Record unacceptable side effects and seek a design that meets both operational and security needs.

Assess effectiveness as a set of claims to verify. If an option filters remote writes, identify the protocols, functions, routes and bypass paths it covers. If it adds an independent sensor, verify its separate power, signal path, calibration and response. If it replaces an unsupported gateway, verify migration of serial mappings, timing, alarms, configurations and recovery artifacts. Define acceptance criteria before procurement or implementation. A control cannot receive full residual-risk credit merely because its project has been funded.

Consider lifecycle cost and complexity. Purchase price is only one component; include engineering, testing, outage coordination, licensing, training, monitoring, certificate and rule maintenance, spare parts, vendor support and eventual replacement. Complexity can create risk when the organization cannot maintain the control correctly. A sophisticated application gateway with no supported protocol model or trained owner may underperform a simpler well-maintained boundary for the actual requirement. Evaluate maintainability and evidence production as part of effectiveness, not as administrative afterthoughts.

Temporary compensating controls require an explicit end condition. If a patch needs a future outage, an interim restriction may reduce exposure, but its scope, validation, owner, monitoring and expiry must be recorded. Identify what would invalidate the exception, such as a new bypass path, a public exploit matching the installed conditions or failure of the compensating control. Expiry should trigger action or escalation rather than silently extending itself. Repeated extensions can become an unmanaged permanent architecture and need accountable review.

Document the selected option and the rejected alternatives with reasons. Keep forecast residual risk separate from current risk until implementation and validation are complete. Assign treatment ownership, milestones, dependencies and the acceptance authority for any retained risk. Define how the control will be monitored after commissioning and how future changes enter reassessment. The result is a risk treatment plan that a design/implementation team can execute and an operations team can sustain, with clear evidence showing whether the intended reduction was achieved.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — TREATMENT OPTIONS (synthetic): Unpatched gateway G permits dangerous remote writes from a vendor path; an approved engineering recovery workflow still needs local writes. Option P: supported firmware patch, four-hour outage, serial polling compatibility test required, earliest approved outage in six weeks. Option F: temporary boundary rule blocks vendor-to-G writes using validated protocol-aware enforcement, preserves approved local engineering, but does not cover a separate cellular bypass. Option R: remove all remote access immediately; vendor can attend locally within 24 hours, while required emergency recovery target is 2 hours. Option N: replace G with a supported model in three months, including map migration, testing and operator training. Proposed exception says 'use F until convenient' and names no owner or expiry. Insurance covers some financial loss but does not change process behavior.
worked_examples.solution:
P can remove the specified software weakness if the fix is applicable and validated, but its six-week lead time leaves a current exposure to manage. F offers a narrower interim reduction only if the cellular bypass is removed or controlled; otherwise the threat can take an uncovered path. Preserve the approved local write workflow deliberately rather than assuming all writes are malicious. R closes the remote path but its 24-hour support arrival conflicts with a two-hour emergency recovery objective unless another qualified local recovery capability exists.

N may address supportability and broader lifecycle concerns, but three months of procurement and migration is not immediate remediation. Its acceptance must include serial mappings, polling timing, alarms and recovery, not only IP reachability. The exception must name an accountable owner, validated interim controls, monitoring, an expiry aligned to the treatment plan and escalation triggers. Insurance is a financial arrangement, not a substitute for preventing or limiting the physical consequence. A defensible plan can combine an actually complete interim boundary treatment with a validated patch or replacement and explicit residual-risk acceptance during the interval.

guided_practice.prompt: Write an interim treatment condition that allows F to be credited only after the cellular path is addressed.
guided_practice.hint: Name the measurable path property, its evidence and the exception boundary.
guided_practice.solution: Before temporary acceptance, demonstrate in the approved representative and site verification process that every vendor path to G traverses the validated write restriction or is disabled, including the cellular gateway. Preserve authorized local recovery and log its use. Assign an owner, monitoring and a fixed expiry tied to the approved patch milestone; a newly discovered bypass or control failure suspends the acceptance pending review.

independent_task.brief: Produce a treatment decision table for P, F, R and N, including side effects, evidence gates, owner and residual exposure during implementation.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: F receives no complete path-coverage credit while the cellular bypass remains.
The two-hour recovery requirement is considered when evaluating remote-access removal.
Temporary exceptions have ownership, validation, expiry and invalidation triggers.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Zone formation from functions, consequences and trust
lessons.body:
A zone is a grouping used to organize assets with common cybersecurity requirements and manage their trust relationships. In an assessment, zone formation should begin with functions, consequences, exposure and required controls. Existing VLANs, subnets, rooms and departments are useful evidence but do not automatically define appropriate zones. A single subnet can contain a read-only historian, a process-changing engineering station and a controller with different consequences and access needs.

Develop the zone model iteratively. Start with the process inventory and initial criticality assessment, identify groups whose requirements are sufficiently similar, then examine communications and administrative dependencies. Separate business functions from process functions where their trust and exposure differ. Consider safety-related functions, maintenance access, wireless or portable systems, external supplier connections and shared infrastructure explicitly. Do not force every device into one broad OT zone merely because it belongs to the facilities organization.

Common requirements do not mean unlimited trust within a zone. Local authentication, least privilege, hardening and monitoring can remain necessary. A zone boundary is an architectural abstraction; enforcement may involve firewalls, application gateways, physical separation, endpoint controls, controlled transfer procedures or combinations. Describe which mechanism enforces each relevant communication requirement. A colored box in a diagram is not evidence that the grouped assets are isolated from others or equally protected internally.

Identify assets that serve multiple zones. Shared directory, time, virtualization, storage and backup services can become cross-zone dependencies and administrative common causes. Decide whether they belong in a dedicated shared-service zone, have per-zone instances, or require another architecture based on requirements and feasibility. The assessment should expose the dependency and needed protections rather than assume shared infrastructure is neutral. Management planes deserve particular attention because a single administration path can alter several nominally separated process zones.

Use consequence and capability to challenge groupings. An independent protective relay may need a different treatment from supervisory metering because it provides a distinct protective function and has different acceptable access. A vendor jump host should not inherit the same trust as the controllers it maintains simply because it needs temporary reachability. A historian's normal read purpose does not justify placing an externally reachable historian directly with critical controllers if its management and software exposure differs. Analyze what a compromise of one member allows against the others.

Preserve legitimate operational communications as explicit requirements. Over-segmentation without understanding discovery, time, multicast, serial gateways or recovery can break required functions and encourage bypasses. Under-segmentation can make a low-consequence endpoint a foothold into high-consequence control. The assessment should document proposed zones, membership rationale, required cross-zone communications, shared dependencies, target protection needs and uncertainty. Detailed design later selects enforcement mechanisms and validates behavior.

Zone models also need lifecycle ownership. A new virtual machine, portable engineering laptop or wireless bridge can change the trust boundary without adding a new cabinet. Define how assets enter and leave zones, who approves communication changes and how diagrams are reconciled with actual configuration. Link each zone to the risk scenarios and cybersecurity requirements that justified it. This prevents the model from becoming a static picture detached from commissioning, operations and recovery.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — ZONE DRAFT (synthetic): One existing VLAN 120 contains EPMS meters M, protective relays P, historian H, engineering jump host J and cooling controller B. H has an enterprise-facing web interface. J permits vendor maintenance and stores project credentials. P's protective logic continues locally and requires tightly controlled configuration access. M needs periodic read polling; B needs supervisory setpoint control from a specific application. All VMs share directory D and hypervisor management V. The draft labels the entire VLAN Facilities Trusted and claims no internal restrictions are necessary. A proposal separates meters, protective functions, supervisory applications, maintenance access and shared services, but has not yet documented required cross-zone flows.
worked_examples.solution:
The existing VLAN groups assets with materially different functions, privileges and exposure. H's enterprise-facing service and J's vendor maintenance role can introduce footholds into the same addressing domain as protective and cooling functions. The label Facilities Trusted does not remove the need for effective authorization or restrict lateral communication. P's local protective role and configuration sensitivity deserve explicit requirements distinct from routine meter polling.

The proposed functional separation is a useful assessment hypothesis, not a completed secure architecture. It must preserve required polling, supervisory control, time, authentication, engineering and recovery communications through justified conduits. D and V remain shared administrative dependencies that can cross the new zone boundaries; separating data-plane VLANs alone does not isolate a common privileged hypervisor administrator. Record each zone's membership rationale, consequences, allowed functions and ownership, then derive testable communication and management requirements for IC34 design work.

guided_practice.prompt: A team places all assets with the same vendor name into one zone. Explain when that might be insufficient and propose better grouping evidence.
guided_practice.hint: Product branding is not the same as a common operational trust requirement.
guided_practice.solution: One supplier may provide meters, protective relays, engineering tools and externally managed gateways with very different capabilities and consequences. Group using required security properties, process function, exposure, administrative authority and acceptable communications. Vendor compatibility can influence implementation, but should not override a demonstrated trust or consequence difference.

independent_task.brief: Produce a proposed zone register for the supplied assets, including shared D/V dependencies and the evidence needed before design approval.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Membership follows security requirements and process consequences rather than VLAN or department alone.
Internal controls and cross-zone management dependencies remain visible.
Required communications are identified for subsequent conduit design.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Conduit analysis and communication requirement matrices
lessons.body:
A conduit represents a controlled communication relationship between zones. Its specification must describe the actual exchanges needed by the system, not just draw an arrow labeled TCP/IP. For every relationship, record source and destination roles, initiator, responder, protocol and service, application function, direction of data and commands, authentication, confidentiality/integrity needs, expected timing, availability, monitoring, owner and failure behavior. Add implementation addresses later or alongside the functional roles so that routine renumbering does not erase the requirement's meaning.

Distinguish connection initiation from information direction. A historian can initiate a TCP connection to a gateway and receive measurement data in response. A stateful firewall may allow the returning packets as part of the established session without requiring a separate broad gateway-initiated rule. A stateless policy needs appropriate explicit handling of both directions, with careful source/destination ports and platform behavior. Do not copy an example rule between these models without understanding its semantics. Also distinguish a bidirectional transport session from the permitted application operations: a read transaction still exchanges packets both ways.

Define the smallest justified service scope. A requirement for meter reads does not justify every function carried on the same port. A requirement for software updates does not justify permanent unrestricted internet access from a controller. Where protocol-aware enforcement is unavailable or unsupported, identify endpoint authorization, intermediary design or operational restrictions that meet the requirement, and record any remaining gap. Encryption can protect a conduit but can also reduce network inspection visibility; decide where authenticated application logs or controlled termination provide necessary evidence.

Account for ancillary services and operating phases. Name resolution, time, identity, licensing, certificate renewal, backups, monitoring and recovery can be critical even when they are absent from the normal process-flow diagram. Some traffic is needed only during commissioning or maintenance and should not remain broadly available without justification. Broadcast and multicast discovery may not cross routed boundaries; replacing a flat network with segmentation can therefore affect device discovery or application operation. Document a supported alternative rather than allowing every broadcast simply to make a test pass.

Evaluate all address families and paths. An IPv4-only policy does not establish IPv6 isolation if the hosts have active IPv6 connectivity. A second NIC, cellular gateway, serial maintenance link or portable laptop can create another conduit. Address translation changes the identities visible to enforcement and logs, so specify whether rules use pre- or post-translation values according to the actual platform. A wildcard subnet may inadvertently include future or unrelated assets. Use role-based requirements with controlled object membership and verify the implemented match.

Timing and failure behavior belong in the matrix. A measurement consumer may need data younger than a specified age and an explicit bad-quality indication when that cannot be met. A time conduit may require bounded offset and behavior during loss, while a maintenance conduit may safely fail closed. Define retry, queue and reconnect behavior where delays can affect process state. A store-and-forward gateway must not deliver an obsolete command as though it were a current authorized action after a long outage unless the application protocol explicitly validates freshness and state.

The assessment output is a justified communication matrix plus a gap analysis against the observed architecture. Every allowed relationship should map to a required function and an owner; every observed but unapproved relationship should be investigated. Denied relationships should have a rationale and a validation method. The matrix becomes input to detailed design, firewall/application policy, logging and factory/site acceptance tests. It should also define how exceptions and changes are approved so that the implemented conduit does not gradually expand beyond its assessed purpose.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — COMMUNICATION REQUIREMENTS (synthetic): H historian initiates TCP/502 to G for Modbus function 3 reads only; responses return on the established session. J engineering host may use function 6/16 to G only during approved maintenance. G must not initiate new sessions to H. T time server supplies time to H and J; maximum accepted clock offset for event correlation is 1 second. Enterprise E may read H's published HTTPS report through proxy P; E must not reach G directly. H and G have IPv6 enabled, but the draft firewall rules mention only IPv4. A queued engineering command older than 5 seconds must be rejected. The current draft rule says allow H subnet→G any TCP and allow G→H subnet any TCP for replies.
worked_examples.solution:
The draft over-permits both directions. H needs the justified Modbus read function, not arbitrary TCP services, and G's responses should be handled by the chosen firewall's supported session behavior rather than a broad new-session permission. A port-only TCP/502 rule still does not implement function-3-only authorization; identify the application-aware or endpoint mechanism needed to restrict writes. J's separate maintenance function requires its own identity, approval and time conditions.

The conduit model must include T because event ordering depends on a one-second clock-quality requirement. E's report access terminates through P and must not become direct G reachability. IPv6 is a known policy gap, not an abstract possibility: both endpoints enable it while the draft controls only IPv4. The five-second command-age rule needs application-level timestamp or sequence/state validation at an appropriate trusted point; network connectivity alone cannot establish freshness. These requirements can be turned into positive and negative acceptance tests in the design course.

guided_practice.prompt: Write one positive and one negative acceptance test for each of H–G, E–P–H and the queued-command requirement.
guided_practice.hint: Test required behavior and a nearby forbidden behavior, with the relevant layer made explicit.
guided_practice.solution: H–G: an authorized function-3 read succeeds with a valid response; a function-16 write from H is rejected by the specified application-aware or endpoint control. E–P–H: approved report access succeeds through P; a direct E-to-G attempt is denied on both active address families. Queue: a valid current command within five seconds is processed under its authorization; an otherwise valid command older than five seconds is rejected and logged without process action.

independent_task.brief: Create a complete conduit matrix and a paired permitted/forbidden test list for the supplied requirements.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Initiation, return traffic and application functions are distinct.
IPv4/IPv6 and ancillary time dependencies are included.
Command freshness is assigned to a mechanism capable of evaluating it.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.
