lessons.title: Security targets, capability claims and achieved assurance
lessons.body:
Security-level terminology helps separate what a system needs from what a component can support and what the implemented system actually demonstrates. In the ISA/IEC 62443 family, target, capability and achieved concepts are distinct. This original lesson explains the engineering distinction using public course scope and public guidance; formal definitions, applicable requirements and conformance determinations require the licensed standard edition and qualified interpretation. The programme does not reproduce normative requirement clauses or award a security-level certification.

A target expresses the required protection for a zone or conduit in its risk and operating context. It follows from the credible threat capabilities, consequences, existing conditions and risk criteria. It is not obtained by rounding a CVSS score, multiplying an ordinal matrix or selecting the largest number available on a product brochure. The assessment must explain why the selected protection is appropriate and translate it into requirements that the design team can implement and verify.

A capability claim concerns what a component or system can support within a stated scope and configuration. A certified component may support functions relevant to a target, but the integrator must verify the certificate's exact product, version, functions, assumptions and exclusions. Capability does not mean that every function is enabled, configured correctly or used through every path. A strong firewall component cannot compensate automatically for an unrestricted physical maintenance port, a shared administrator identity or untrusted recovery artifacts elsewhere in the system.

An achieved claim concerns the implemented arrangement and its evidence against the applicable requirements. It requires more than an inventory of capable products. The architecture, configuration, integration, operating procedures, identity lifecycle, monitoring, maintenance and recovery must satisfy the relevant system requirements under the assessed conditions. Record gaps and deviations explicitly. A successful factory test can support part of the evidence while leaving site-specific routing, dependencies, physical access and operational response to be validated later.

Protection needs can differ across foundational security functions. Public discussions commonly organize these around identification/authentication, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events and resource availability. A vector can express differentiated targets rather than pretending one scalar describes every dimension equally. The vector is not an invitation to choose arbitrary numbers: each dimension still needs a justified target and the applicable requirement set. Do not average dimensions to hide a weakness in a critical function.

Security-level concepts are separate from functional-safety integrity levels and from simple maturity scores. A cybersecurity target does not establish the probability of a dangerous hardware failure, validate a safety function or certify a person's competence. Likewise, an organization's mature process does not prove that one deployed conduit enforces its required command restrictions. These dimensions can inform one another through engineering evidence while remaining distinct assurance questions.

The assessment output should state the target rationale, scope, assumptions, required security properties, evidence needed for capability claims and the unresolved gaps preventing an achieved conclusion. Link requirements to scenarios and planned acceptance tests. Where the relevant licensed clauses have not been checked, label the result an authored engineering requirement set pending normative review, not full standard compliance. This protects the usefulness of the work: the design team receives concrete objectives, and the owner sees what is known, what is merely claimed and what remains to be demonstrated.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — ASSURANCE CASE (synthetic; vector labels are local teaching shorthand, not a normative conformance result): Zone Z has proposed target vector [2,2,2,1,3,2,2] across identification/authentication, use control, system integrity, confidentiality, restricted data flow, event response and resource availability. Firewall product F has a supplier certificate claiming capability within a specified firmware/configuration scope, but its deployed firmware has not been matched to that scope. A local maintenance port bypasses F. Event-response procedure has not been exercised. An assessor proposes averaging the vector to 2 and declaring the whole zone achieved level 2 because F is certified. The site has not completed licensed requirement-by-requirement review or site acceptance testing.
worked_examples.solution:
The proposed vector preserves a higher restricted-data-flow target than confidentiality, but it is only a target proposal with a rationale still needed for each dimension. Averaging the values loses that difference and cannot establish achieved assurance. F's certificate requires exact scope matching; an unmatched deployed firmware cannot simply inherit the supplier claim. Even a matching capable firewall would not address the bypass port or prove event-response performance.

The defensible conclusion is that Z has a proposed differentiated requirement target and unresolved implementation/evidence gaps. Resolve the bypass, define and exercise event response, match component claims to deployed versions, complete the applicable licensed requirement review and perform the necessary integration/site verification before making an achieved claim. None of this produces a SIL determination or an ISA specialist certificate for the learner. The assessment's role is to make the target and evidence obligations explicit for secure design and accountable acceptance.

guided_practice.prompt: A procurement team asks whether buying a component with a higher capability label automatically raises the zone target or achieved result. Explain both distinctions.
guided_practice.hint: A requirement, a supported capability and an implemented evidence conclusion answer different questions.
guided_practice.solution: The target follows the zone risk and requirement analysis, not the purchased label. A higher component capability may help satisfy selected requirements but does not automatically change the target. Achieved assurance depends on the integrated configured system meeting the applicable requirements, including paths, procedures and dependencies outside that component; procurement alone establishes neither implementation nor verification.

independent_task.brief: Write an assurance-gap register for Z with separate target, component-capability and implemented-evidence columns.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: The vector is not averaged into a blanket achieved claim.
Supplier certification is checked for exact scope and distinguished from integration evidence.
Normative review, site validation and separate safety assurance remain explicit gates.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Writing a cybersecurity requirements specification
lessons.body:
The cybersecurity requirements specification, or CRS, translates assessment conclusions into obligations for design, implementation and acceptance. It should state the system and baseline in scope, relevant process functions and constraints, zone/conduit model, threat and risk rationale, required security properties, roles, interfaces, verification methods and lifecycle responsibilities. It is not merely a list of products to buy or a copied control catalog. Requirements must be sufficiently precise that the designer can choose a suitable mechanism and the owner can determine whether the result meets the need.

Write one assessable obligation per requirement where possible. Identify the responsible system or component, the required behavior, the conditions under which it applies and the measurable criterion. For example: 'The maintenance access service shall terminate an existing vendor session within 60 seconds of an authorized revocation request and shall record the named requester, affected identity, session identifier and result.' This is an original illustrative requirement, not a quoted standard clause. It is stronger than 'remote access shall be secure' because it defines observable behavior and evidence.

Keep functional intent distinct from implementation constraints. A requirement to reject unauthorized register writes describes the necessary behavior; specifying a particular firewall model is a design choice unless procurement or compatibility imposes that constraint. Some environments need explicit platform constraints, but document why. Avoid choosing a product before understanding whether it can inspect the protocol, preserve required timing and cover every route. A requirement can name a supported mechanism where essential while still stating the outcome that must be verified.

Link each requirement to its source. Sources include risk scenarios, process and recovery objectives, owner policies, applicable contractual/regulatory obligations and licensed standard requirements. Use identifiers so that a reviewer can move from a risk to the requirement, the implementing design, the test and the result. A requirement with no rationale may be unnecessary or poorly scoped; a severe assessed scenario with no treatment requirement may be an omission. Record normative references only when the applicable licensed text and edition have actually been reviewed. Public course topics do not establish clause-level compliance.

Define positive, negative and degraded-state tests. A read-only historian requirement needs proof that authorized reads work and unauthorized writes fail. A remote-access requirement needs approved session success, unapproved access denial, revocation and relevant outage behavior. A recovery requirement needs a complete trusted restoration under the required dependency-loss scenario, not just a file-copy test. Include instrumentation, baseline, expected results, tolerances, evidence retention and responsibility. Tests must be designed safely and executed only in authorized environments.

Account for timing, data quality and process compatibility. Specify maximum command age, measurement freshness, clock offset, permitted downtime, recovery objectives and required local operation during communication loss where relevant. Security controls can fail by blocking necessary operation or by silently allowing stale or unauthenticated data. State how invalid data is indicated and what the consumer does. Avoid ambiguous adjectives such as fast, robust or adequate unless another requirement defines their measurable meaning.

The CRS should also define operation and change obligations. Identify who maintains accounts, trust stores, signatures, rules, logs, backups and support baselines; how exceptions are approved; which changes trigger reassessment; and what evidence is handed over. Track requirement status through proposed, agreed, implemented, verified and accepted states rather than calling every drafted statement complete. A well-formed CRS allows IC34 design work to proceed with clear security and operational requirements while preserving unresolved assumptions for accountable resolution.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — CRS REVIEW EXTRACT (synthetic): R-01 'The OT network shall be secure.' R-02 'Install vendor Firewall Q.' R-03 'H shall perform function-3 reads from G; H-originated function-6/16 writes shall be rejected and logged on every active path/address family.' R-04 'Vendor session revocation shall complete within 60 seconds of an authorized request, including already active sessions.' R-05 'EPMS recovery shall meet RTO 90 minutes from detection and historian RPO 15 minutes, including loss of D1.' Test T-03 currently checks only that H can read; T-04 checks only denial of new login; T-05 copies one backup file while D1 remains online. Risk K-7 concerns a cellular bypass, but no requirement references it. No owner is assigned to certificate renewal.
worked_examples.solution:
R-01 is not directly testable because secure has no defined behavior or criterion. R-02 names a product but does not establish what that product must enforce or why it is suitable. R-03 is a stronger behavior requirement, but T-03 covers only the positive read case and omits write rejection, logging, alternate paths and IPv6. R-04 explicitly includes existing sessions, so T-04's new-login denial is incomplete. R-05 includes identity-service loss and both time/data objectives; copying one file with D1 healthy does not validate that restoration.

K-7 needs a traced requirement that removes, controls or otherwise treats the cellular route under the approved risk decision. Certificate renewal needs a named operational owner, supported procedure and expiry/validation criteria where certificates support required functions. Build a traceability table linking K-7 and the other scenarios to requirements, design mechanisms and paired tests. Preserve the distinction between a drafted requirement, implemented mechanism, verified behavior and formal owner acceptance.

guided_practice.prompt: Rewrite R-01 into two measurable requirements addressing unauthorized engineering access and stale telemetry.
guided_practice.hint: Name the actor/function, condition, response and evidence rather than using a general adjective.
guided_practice.solution: Example: the engineering access service shall permit process-changing sessions only for named approved identities within an authorized maintenance condition, reject all other attempts and record the decision with trusted time. The telemetry consumer shall mark data older than the approved maximum age invalid within the defined detection interval and shall not present it as current good-quality data. The owner must specify the actual age/interval and supported degraded behavior before acceptance testing.

independent_task.brief: Produce a CRS excerpt with eight original requirements, each traced to a risk, operational constraint, design responsibility and acceptance test.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Requirements define observable behavior and applicable conditions.
Positive, forbidden and degraded-state cases cover the stated scope.
Unresolved parameters and normative-review status are explicit rather than invented.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Assessment reporting, evidence integrity and finding closure
lessons.body:
An assessment report should answer the owner's decision question and preserve the evidence needed to challenge the answer. Provide an executive explanation of the material scenarios, consequences, current limitations and required decisions, then a technical record of scope, baseline, methods, coverage, evidence, findings, risk reasoning, zone/conduit model and treatment requirements. Different readers need different detail, but the executive conclusion must not contradict the technical limitations or quietly upgrade a forecast into a verified result.

A finding should distinguish observation from inference. 'The exported rule R1 permits J to C on any TCP port' is an observed configuration fact within the export's provenance. 'A compromised J session may reach the controller management service' is an inference requiring route, service and authorization context. 'The controller was compromised' is an incident claim requiring separate evidence. State the chain explicitly. Avoid dramatic language that leaps from an exposed service to a confirmed physical consequence, and avoid minimizing a clear configuration defect merely because no incident has been observed.

Give every evidence item a stable identifier. Record source asset, collector, method, date/time and time quality, configuration/version context, file location, integrity digest where appropriate, access restrictions and limitations. Preserve original artifacts and work on controlled analysis copies. A digest helps detect later changes; it does not authenticate the original device or prove the content was truthful. Redact credentials and unnecessary personal data from general report copies while preserving authorized evidence needed for technical review through a controlled channel.

A reproducible finding links to the exact relevant evidence and the analysis method. For a rule-order issue, show the ordered rules, the representative flow and the first-match reasoning. For a timing issue, show the event references, clock corrections and arithmetic. For a vulnerability, show component version, feature condition and advisory revision. A screenshot without source, date or context may be useful illustration but is weak as the sole basis for a baseline-specific conclusion. Retain enough detail that another qualified reviewer can reach or challenge the result without trusting the author's memory.

Use clear status definitions. Open means the assessed condition remains. Planned means a treatment is approved or scheduled but not implemented. Implemented awaiting verification means a change is reported but its required behavior has not been validated. Verified closed means the closure criteria have been met for the stated scenario and baseline. Accepted residual risk is a separate owner decision and may coexist with an open technical weakness under a bounded exception. Do not relabel an accepted weakness as patched or a purchased product as operational.

Closure evidence should match the original finding's mechanism. If the issue is a cellular bypass, a screenshot of the primary firewall's new rule does not prove the bypass is gone. If the issue is stale telemetry marked good, a faster network link does not prove the consumer rejects old data. Re-test the relevant allowed and forbidden behavior, update dependency and consequence assumptions, and check for new regressions. Document who verified the result and whether the verification was analytical, simulated, representative-lab or site observation.

The final report should include uncertainty and dissent that could change the decision, with named evidence owners and follow-up dates. Define report validity conditions and reassessment triggers, especially for changing remote access, firmware, process load and recovery dependencies. Archive the baseline and traceability records so future maintenance can update the assessment instead of starting from an unexplained risk score. A report is complete when it supports an accountable decision and sustainable engineering follow-through, not when every row is colored green.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — FINDING REGISTER (synthetic): F-01 cellular path bypasses reviewed firewall; evidence E-01 physical walkdown and E-02 gateway route export. Treatment status says Closed because a new rule was added only to the primary firewall. F-02 active vendor sessions survive directory disablement; gateway patch purchased but not installed; status says Remediated. F-03 stale telemetry remains good; application freshness rule implemented, but only a normal live-value test performed; status says Verified. E-04 packet trace timestamp is 90 seconds fast; report uses uncorrected times. E-05 configuration export digest differs from the original manifest; cause not investigated. Director accepted F-04's residual risk until 2026-10-31 under a named compensating control.
worked_examples.solution:
F-01's closure does not address the bypass path demonstrated by E-01/E-02; the primary firewall rule may be useful elsewhere but is not matching closure evidence. F-02 remains open with treatment planned because purchasing a patch does not install or validate it. F-03 is implemented awaiting verification: a normal live-value test does not exercise stale-data behavior or the required quality transition.

Correct E-04's time analysis using the documented offset while retaining original timestamps. E-05's digest mismatch requires investigation of whether the artifact changed, the wrong file was referenced or the manifest is incorrect; it is not automatic proof of malicious tampering, but integrity cannot be assumed. F-04 is an accepted residual-risk exception with an expiry and conditions, not necessarily a technically remediated weakness. The report should preserve these distinctions and make outstanding evidence work visible to the owner.

guided_practice.prompt: Write a corrected status and closure criterion for F-03.
guided_practice.hint: Test the defect that motivated the change, not only the normal path.
guided_practice.solution: Status: implemented, awaiting verification. Closure requires an authorized test that withholds or ages telemetry beyond the configured bound, confirms the consumer changes quality/indication within the specified interval and does not present stale values as current good data, records the event, and restores normal behavior when valid fresh telemetry resumes without hiding the interruption.

independent_task.brief: Prepare a five-finding technical report excerpt with evidence references, observation/inference separation, status and mechanism-matched closure criteria.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Purchased, implemented, verified and accepted are distinct statuses.
Time correction and evidence-integrity discrepancies are handled transparently.
Every closure test addresses the original technical condition and baseline.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Facilitated assessment workshops and evidence-based challenge
lessons.body:
A useful assessment workshop brings together the people who understand the process, controls, network, identity, safety, operations, maintenance and supplier interfaces. The facilitator's task is to make their evidence and assumptions compatible enough to support a decision. A meeting in which the loudest participant supplies every rating can produce a tidy register with little technical validity. Plan the agenda around the system functions and scenarios, and send the current diagrams, inventory, criteria and evidence questions in advance.

Begin by confirming the decision, scope, baseline and rules of engagement. State which activities the workshop may authorize and which require a separate operational approval. Reviewing an architecture does not authorize a participant to run a scanner during the meeting. Identify the process owner for consequences, the controls engineer for device behavior, the network/identity owners for paths and privileges, the safety specialist for protective-function assumptions and the operator for actual response workflows. One person may hold several roles, but the evidence responsibilities should remain clear.

Walk one scenario end to end before assigning a rating. Ask the group to identify the initiating condition, access path, action, process effect, safeguards and time to consequence. Use a live evidence table with columns for fact, source, assumption, disputed point, owner and follow-up. A claim such as 'the historian is read-only' should be refined into effective account rights, protocol functions and actual route enforcement. A claim such as 'operators will respond immediately' should be refined into alarm delivery, staffing, diagnosis and action times. The facilitator should ask precise questions without turning uncertainty into personal blame.

Structured assessment tools can help organize scope, questions and recommendations. CISA's official CSET project describes a tool that collects facility-specific information and compares it with selected standards/guidance to support cybersecurity improvement. Treat its outputs as dependent on the selected scope, content and supplied answers. This programme does not execute CSET or reproduce its standards content. If learners use an approved current release in an isolated environment, they should record the version, selected assessment basis and evidence behind each answer; generated reports do not independently prove packet filtering, controller behavior or formal certification.

Resolve disagreement by separating different propositions. The network team may correctly state that a firewall blocks enterprise traffic while the controls team correctly observes that a local service laptop reaches the same controller. The claims concern different paths. The safety team may credit a local trip for loss of network communications but not for a shared sensor-power failure. Do not average these statements into one generic effectiveness percentage. Update the scenario and control scope, then request the specific evidence needed to close the disagreement.

Use decision gates and a parking list. Some issues can be resolved from available evidence during the workshop; others need a configuration export, representative test, supplier clarification or qualified process study. Record unresolved items with an owner, due date and the decision they block. Avoid spending the entire meeting debating a minor naming discrepancy while a high-consequence unknown remains untouched. At the same time, do not suppress a credible minority concern simply to reach consensus before the scheduled end.

End with an agreed record of what was established and what remains conditional. Confirm scenario descriptions, provisional ratings, zone/conduit changes, requirements, treatment owners and acceptance/escalation routes. Read back important assumptions and dissent. The facilitator should ensure that the resulting actions are technically specific: 'verify active-session revocation under D1 loss' is actionable, while 'improve security' is not. Follow-up review should examine evidence and decisions, not merely whether an action owner marked a task complete.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — WORKSHOP RECORD (synthetic; no CSET execution): Operations says cooling can run locally for 30 minutes without the BMS. Controls says a 10-minute high-load condition requires load reduction if both cooling trains fail. Network says enterprise-to-controller traffic is blocked by F. Maintenance demonstrates an approved diagram of laptop L connected directly to the controller service port. IT says disabling a vendor in D1 removes access; gateway documentation says existing sessions remain valid for 8 hours. A questionnaire answer says backups are tested because a file was copied successfully; the recovery objective requires full service in 90 minutes without D1. Safety representative is absent. Sponsor asks the workshop to approve an active scan immediately to settle all disputes before lunch.
worked_examples.solution:
The cooling statements may concern different failures: loss of BMS supervision while local control continues is not the same as loss of both cooling trains under high load. Separate the scenarios and ask the process/safety owners to validate their operating assumptions. The network and maintenance claims likewise concern different paths; F's enterprise restriction does not cover L's direct service connection. The identity contradiction is specific: D1 disablement blocks some new authentication but gateway sessions have a separate lifetime.

The backup questionnaire answer is too broad for the stated recovery objective because file copying does not demonstrate full restoration without D1. Reclassify it with an evidence gap and assign a representative recovery test. The absent safety representative prevents the group from claiming that safety-related assumptions have been qualified merely by consensus. The requested scan needs its own authorized method, target, safety limits and recovery plan; a meeting deadline does not provide those. The workshop can produce a precise action plan and bounded conclusions without fabricating certainty or performing unapproved tests.

guided_practice.prompt: Write five follow-up actions from the workshop, each with a technical question, evidence owner and decision affected.
guided_practice.hint: Use the conflicting claims to identify the missing proposition rather than asking for generic confirmation.
guided_practice.solution: Process owner: distinguish BMS-loss and dual-train-loss thermal limits, affecting consequence ratings. Network/maintenance owners: trace L service-port authorization and reach, affecting conduit coverage. Identity/gateway owners: verify active-session revocation, affecting vendor offboarding requirements. Recovery owner: demonstrate full EPMS restore without D1, affecting RTO assurance. Safety specialist: review protection independence and high-load assumptions, affecting qualified consequence acceptance.

independent_task.brief: Facilitate a scripted assessment using the supplied roles; retain disagreements and convert them into evidence tasks and provisional requirements.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Different failure scenarios and access paths are not averaged together.
Questionnaire answers are supported or qualified with technical evidence.
The workshop does not invent safety approval or active-test authority.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

lessons.title: Maintaining risk through commissioning, operation and recovery
lessons.body:
An assessment is a baseline-specific engineering argument that must be maintained as the system changes. Its useful lifetime depends on the assumptions behind the conclusion, not simply the date on the cover. A controller replacement, new remote-access path, changed load profile, modified alarm logic, revised vendor advisory or loss of a compensating control can invalidate a risk decision before the next scheduled annual review. Define both periodic review and event-driven triggers.

Commissioning should reconcile the as-designed and as-built systems. Verify asset identities, firmware, zone membership, communication paths, effective accounts, approved project files and test results against the CRS. A temporary commissioning rule or vendor modem can remain after handover if no one owns its removal. Track temporary states explicitly and make their closure an acceptance condition where required. A factory test performed on one version or topology does not automatically cover the installed site's changed dependencies.

Operations needs indicators tied to the control assumptions. If residual risk depends on all vendor access traversing a gateway, monitor for bypass connections and reconcile approved remote paths. If recovery depends on a valid certificate or available offline backup, monitor expiry and restoration readiness. If manual response is credited, retain training, staffing and exercise evidence relevant to the required timing. Dashboards should show the failure of an assumption, not merely the number of completed administrative tasks.

Maintenance and optimization can change security behavior. Firmware updates may alter services, logging or protocol support. A performance optimization that disables inspection or increases a queue age can invalidate command-integrity requirements. Moving a VM to shared storage may remove a recovery independence assumption. Evaluate change impact by tracing the changed asset or requirement through scenarios, dependencies, tests and acceptance decisions. Reuse still-applicable evidence and refresh what changed; neither blindly keeping everything nor restarting every assessment from zero is efficient.

Troubleshooting requires controlled exceptions. An engineer may need temporary diagnostic access, increased logging or a service restart. Record the purpose, scope, duration, approval, compensating measures and rollback. Verify that the temporary rule, account or cable is removed when the task ends. The urgency of restoring service does not make permanent untracked bypasses acceptable. Capture enough evidence to understand what was changed so that the final baseline and risk model remain accurate.

Incident response and recovery create a different evidence challenge. The pre-incident assessment can help identify critical functions and dependencies, but incident facts may reveal an attack path or control failure that the model missed. Preserve evidence under the response plan, reassess the trust of credentials, images and backups, and restore to a validated known-good state rather than merely the most recent state. After recovery, review which assumptions failed, update requirements and validate the corrective controls. A successful reboot is not the same as restored trust or closed root cause.

The maintained risk register should link each scenario to current assets, requirements, controls, evidence dates, owners, treatment status, acceptance conditions and triggers. Changes should create a review trail showing why a conclusion stayed valid or changed. Feed lessons into design, implementation, commissioning, operations, maintenance, optimization, troubleshooting, incident response and recovery. This is the contribution of IC33 to the intended engineering identity: a repeatable ability to turn uncertain system evidence into justified requirements and accountable decisions. It remains one specialist capability within the broader programme and does not substitute for external ISA course/exam completion or real supervised engineering practice.

worked_examples.title: Worked engineering case
worked_examples.scenario: SYNTHETIC CASE — LIFECYCLE CHANGE LOG (synthetic): Day 0 acceptance assumes all vendor sessions traverse R, firmware G=2.10, backup B is independently administered, and summer load is at most 70%. Day 15 troubleshooting adds a temporary cellular path expiring Day 17; it is still connected on Day 25. Day 20 G is replaced with the same model at version 2.8 and old IP; serial number changes. Day 22 backup administration is merged into the production service account. Day 24 load rises to 90%. Day 25 a new advisory affects enabled write service on 2.8. Operations dashboard shows 100% training completion and last year's successful restore. No change-impact review has updated the risk register. Incident team later finds a project modification predating the newest backup.
worked_examples.solution:
Several acceptance assumptions have changed independently. The expired cellular connection breaks the all-sessions-through-R condition. The replacement is a new asset instance despite the reused IP, and its firmware changes vulnerability applicability. Merging backup administration weakens the previously credited independent recovery path. Higher load can shorten process response margins. The advisory creates a new evidence trigger that matches the installed 2.8/write-service conditions only after those feature facts are verified.

Training completion and an old restore success do not resolve these current technical changes. The risk owner needs an impact review, updated baseline and treatment/acceptance decisions for the affected scenarios. During incident recovery, the newest backup may include the unauthorized project change, so select and validate a trustworthy recovery point using timeline and configuration evidence. The assessment should be updated with the newly learned path and failed assumptions after immediate response activities are handled under the response plan. Do not report the old acceptance as current simply because its signed document still exists.

guided_practice.prompt: Choose three change-log entries and specify the exact prior evidence or acceptance assumption each invalidates, plus the required new evidence.
guided_practice.hint: Follow the changed fact through the original control or consequence argument.
guided_practice.solution: Cellular path invalidates complete R mediation; obtain current physical/routing evidence and verify removal or approved enforcement. Replacement invalidates old serial/firmware applicability; obtain current component versions, feature settings and advisory match. Backup-account merge invalidates administrative independence; obtain effective permissions and validate protected recovery access/copies. Higher load additionally requires refreshed process-time and response-margin evidence from the qualified owners.

independent_task.brief: Prepare a maintained assessment package containing updated inventory, changed assumptions, scenario impacts, requirements, evidence tasks and bounded decisions for the change log.
deliverables: An evidence table distinguishing supplied facts, assumptions and unknowns.
A technically reasoned decision and a reproducible verification or validation procedure.
acceptance_criteria: Reused IP does not hide replacement identity or firmware change.
Each changed assumption is linked to a specific reassessment and evidence task.
Incident recovery distinguishes newest backup from validated known-good state.
independent_task.limitations: Synthetic analytical work only. No real device, process safety claim, vendor command execution, standard conformance determination or credential is implied.

cards.back: A material change to assets, paths, threats, process conditions, safeguards, evidence or acceptance assumptions.

cards.back: A recent backup can preserve an unauthorized change or compromise; provenance, timeline and validation determine trust.

cards.front: How does IC33 feed the lifecycle?
cards.back: It supplies maintained risk reasoning, traceable requirements, evidence gaps and accountable decisions across design through recovery.

questions.prompt: What is the main defect in excluding D1 solely because IT administers it?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. Directory administration is outside the OT team's control. The sponsor asks whether vendor remote maintenance may be enabled before summer. Approved collection: read-only configuration exports and a 20-minute passive mirror-port capture on OT switch S1. No active packets are authorized. Cooling alarms must remain visible; the duty operator may stop collection. The facility director owns acceptance of service interruption risk; the assessor reports findings. A draft scope excludes D1 because it is 'an IT asset'.
options: It would make the cooling controllers physically part of the corporate server rack
The assessment would omit a trust dependency that can authorize OT engineering access
It would prove that directory failures cannot affect the cooling trains
It would prevent the assessor from automatically scanning every IT server
explanations: Logical trust does not change physical location.
Administrative ownership does not remove the directory from the attack-path and consequence model.
The stated authentication dependency suggests the opposite.
Dependency inclusion does not create scanning authority.

questions.prompt: Which proposed action exceeds the current collection authorization?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. options: Reading an owner-provided S1 configuration export
Reviewing a capture from the approved mirror port
Asking the directory owner for authentication policy evidence
Running an ARP discovery sweep from the capture laptop
explanations: The charter explicitly permits read-only exports.
This is the approved passive collection method when implemented as authorized.
Requesting evidence does not probe the directory.
ARP discovery transmits active packets and is not covered by passive capture permission.

questions.prompt: Who can accept the residual service interruption risk in the supplied charter?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. options: The assessor who discovered the highest severity finding
The facility director
The vendor who supplied the remote-access gateway

explanations: Discovery and analysis do not confer risk acceptance authority.
The charter assigns this business and operational accountability to that role.
A supplier does not automatically own the facility's consequence decision.

questions.prompt: Why should summer operating conditions be recorded as an assessment assumption?

They determine which Ethernet MAC addresses are valid
They establish that cyber events can occur only during summer

A consequence modifier is not an exclusive threat window.

questions.prompt: Which revision makes the sponsor's request assessable?

questions.prompt: Which statement is an objective stop condition for the passive collection plan?

explanations: This is an observable service condition tied to the charter's operational constraint.

Waiting for harm defeats a preventive stop mechanism.
Observed packets are the intended input, not inherently a disruption indicator.

questions.prompt: What should a scope register say about D1?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. questions.prompt: A new remote gateway firmware is installed after evidence collection. What should happen before approval?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. Keep every conclusion unchanged because the assessment date is already recorded
Treat the upgrade as proof that all previous vulnerabilities are fixed
Discard the entire inventory even if hardware identities are unchanged
explanations: Change impact determines whether prior evidence still supports the decision.
A timestamp does not preserve applicability after relevant changes.
An upgrade can change exposure without guaranteeing complete remediation.
Refresh affected evidence proportionately rather than deleting unaffected facts.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in the consequence boundary even if it is not an electronic asset?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. options: Only the scanner workstation's operating system
Every corporate office worldwide without a demonstrated dependency
A neighboring hall affected by the shared cooling loop
The vendor support portal solely because the supplier owns it, without establishing any system dependency
explanations: That workstation is not the complete set of affected functions.
Consequence scope requires a reasoned causal connection.
Consequence scope follows possible harm and service dependencies, not only device inventories.
Supplier ownership alone does not establish that the portal can affect the assessed function; its actual role must be determined.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful acceptance criterion for the proposed remote service?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. explanations: Throughput does not establish privilege, revocation, monitoring or recovery adequacy.
Passive observation duration and method cannot prove absence of vulnerabilities.
Training may contribute but cannot establish the integrated system's behavior.

questions.prompt: Why should likelihood judgments include a time horizon?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — A 6 MW data hall uses two cooling trains. Both train controllers authenticate engineering access through corporate directory D1 and receive time from N1. A one-year horizon guarantees one event per year
The horizon determines the controller's required supply voltage

questions.prompt: How should the Day 17 expiry be handled when the path remains on Day 25?

Treat it as an overdue exception/control failure requiring escalation and a current authorized decision
Delete the expiry date from the record
Assume it automatically renews every eight days
explanations: Operational connectivity is not authorization.
Temporary authorization did not silently become permanent.
That hides the failure to close the temporary state.
No such renewal rule is supplied.

questions.prompt: Why might the newest backup be unsuitable after the incident finding?

questions.prompt: Who should decide whether changed residual risk remains acceptable?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — LIFECYCLE CHANGE LOG (synthetic): Day 0 acceptance assumes all vendor sessions traverse R, firmware G=2.10, backup B is independently administered, and summer load is at most 70%. questions.prompt: What is the purpose of event-driven review alongside periodic review?
questions.exhibit: SYNTHETIC CASE — LIFECYCLE CHANGE LOG (synthetic): Day 0 acceptance assumes all vendor sessions traverse R, firmware G=2.10, backup B is independently administered, and summer load is at most 70%. Every change requires exactly the same full assessment regardless of its scope and affected assumptions
